messages.subject: stan error messages under OSX Mountain Lion vs Ubuntu
messages.subject_clean: stan error messages under OSX Mountain Lion vs Ubuntu
messages.body_plain:
Hi Stan team,

I'm trying to dig into an issue <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!msg/stan-users/ezbkBUfpBuQ/oB8j5FfdTAoJ> that a user had a while back, but which did not get resolved. The main problem is, when I run my stan model on mac OSX the error messages are not informative. The same exact code spits out decipherable error messages on Linux.

Compare this:
(OSX 10.8.4, R 3.0.1, RStan 1.3.0, Rcpp_0.10.4, g++ 4.8.1)

> TRANSLATING MODEL 'LTLhfit2' FROM Stan CODE TO C++ CODE NOW.
> COMPILING THE C++ CODE FOR MODEL 'LTLhfit2' NOW.
> SAMPLING FOR MODEL 'LTLhfit2' NOW (CHAIN 1).
> Error in sampler$call_sampler(args_list[[i]]) :
>   c++ exception (unknown reason)
> error occurred during calling the sampler; sampling not done

To:
(Ubuntu 13.04, g++ 4.7.3)

> TRANSLATING MODEL 'LTLhfit2' FROM Stan CODE TO C++ CODE NOW.
> COMPILING THE C++ CODE FOR MODEL 'LTLhfit2' NOW.
> SAMPLING FOR MODEL 'LTLhfit2' NOW (CHAIN 1).
> Error in eval(expr, envir, enclos) :
>   INDEX OPERATOR [] OUT OF BOUNDS; index=0; lower bound=1; upper bound=9; index position=2; Stim
> error occurred during calling the sampler; sampling not done

 Any thoughts on what might be the cause of this? Have other users experienced this problem?

Thanks in advance,
Angela

No idea what's going on.  I just tried my setup,

The other compiler options may make a difference, too.

Here are the models I tried:

oob.stan
-----------------------------------------
transformed data {
   real x[2];
   x[4] <- 7;
}
parameters {
   real y;
}
model {
   y ~ normal(0,1);
}
----------------------------------------

and

oob2.stan
-----------------------------------------
parameters {
   real y;
}
transformed parameters {
   real x[2];
   x[4] <- 7;

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Installation problem
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Installation problem
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

Thank you very much for the support. After many hours of trial and error. I have my Rcpp installed successfully.

Step 1. Uninstall everything

(1) uninstalled R 2.15.3 and RTools30
(2) delete the folder of R and RTools
(3) edit the Path within Environment variable to remove all RTools path

Step 2. Create another window account which doesn't have admin priviledge (Standard user). I use account with admin priviledge without success and try to use a standard user. Surprise that it work but don't know why.

Step 3. Switch to the new user account and install everything

(1) Install R. I have unclicked the 32 bit version and click the 64 bit version instead. My installation path is  C:\R\R-2.15.3

(2) Install RTools using all the default setting. My installation path is C:\R\Rtools

Step 4. Create a batch file

(1) Create a file named Rgui.bat in the folder C:\R\R-2.15.3\bin\x64 with the below content

set Path=C:\R\Rtools\bin;C:\R\Rtools\gcc-4.6.3\bin
Rgui.exe

Step 5. Run the Rgui.bat and try to run the same code again. It is success.

I don't understand why it work. Anyway, I can proceed with my RStan installation now.

Eric

On Wednesday, July 31, 2013 11:19:42 PM UTC+8, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
>
> On 7/31/13 8:48 AM, Eric Chan wrote:
> > Hi Ben,
> >
> > Thank you very much for the help. I have tried to reinstall everything without the space and start R with the admin
> > privileges. However, I experience the same problem. I have tried to post question to the Rcpp list and hope to get a
> > reply soon. I have spent whole day working on it and want to use RStan as soon as possible.
>
> I'm very sorry to hear that.  Windows has given us no end
> of problems on the development side, too, because the entire
> open source C++ toolchain is so much weaker.
>
> You definitely need to get Rcpp working before you can
> install RStan.   When it's sorted out, could you please post
> back here with what the problem was and what needed to be done
> to fix it?  We're trying to build up the expertise to help more
> people through Windows installs in the future.
>
> For getting help from the Rcpp list, I'd suggest trying
> to include more information on exactly what you did in terms
> of installing and uninstalling applications.  I don't know
> enough about Windows to tell you how to do this exactly,
> but your PATH will also be important.  And as Ben said, this
> looks like it may be a permissions issue, so there's the
> matter of how you are logged in (as a regular user or admin),
> which version of Windows you're using, which version of RTools,
> what kind of shell you're using, and so on.
>
> > Hope that someone who has
> > experience this can give some hints on how to solve it.
>
> I'm afraid that's not me.  The only hint I saw online is that
> it may have something to do with the R_HOME environment variable,
> from Dirk's blog:  http://dirk.eddelbuettel.com/blog/2012/11/05/
>
> I hope the Rcpp list or someone else here can help, but
> as Ben says, you're currently hung up on installing Rcpp, which
> is a pre-requisite for RStan.
>
> - Bob

messages.subject_clean: Using "block" operator in matrices
messages.body_plain:
Hi all!

I have a question about the use of the block operator, since I think that I am not sure how to use it properly (and I get parser errors).

Let us suppose that I have to build a matrix of parameters A, which is 3x3, and that I have other vector of parameters, which is declared as a matrix B, 1x3. As a simple example, I want that (using R notation) A[3,1:2] = B[1,2:3]. I tried to do this,

block(A,3,1,1,2) <- block(B,1,2,1,3), but I always get a parser error,

EXPECTATION FAILURE LOCATION: file=input; line=39, column=9

        block(A,k,1,1,(k-1))    <- block(B,1,index,1,(index+k-2));
        ^-- here

DIAGNOSTIC(S) FROM PARSER:
Warning: integer division implicitly rounds to integer. Found int division: (K * (K - 1)) / 2
 Positive values rounded down, negative values rounded up or down in platform-dependent way.
binary infix operator <= with functional interpretation logical_lt requires arguments or primitive type (int or real), found left type=matrix, right arg type=matrix; no matches for function name="logical_lt"
    arg 0 type=matrix
    arg 1 type=matrix
available function signatures for logical_lt:
0.  logical_lt(int, int) : int
1.  logical_lt(int, real) : int
2.  logical_lt(real, int) : int
3.  logical_lt(real, real) : int
Parser expecting: "}"

If you want to know exactly how I build the matrix, it is, which ends up being the lower triangular elements of a matrix KxK

    int           index;
    index       <- 1;

messages.subject: Suitability of Stan for imputation of multinomial outcomes with hierarchical models
messages.subject_clean: Suitability of Stan for imputation of multinomial outcomes with hierarchical models
messages.body_plain:
Hi, everyone.  I have a relatively well-defned initial question, and
then some progressively broader issues.

The manual says "Stan 1.0 does not do discrete sampling."  I'm trying to
figure out the implications of that for using Stan to do imputation of
multinomial outcomes with hierarchical models.  I think it means that
Stan will not allow a discrete variable to be among the values whose
distribution it estimates, i.e., one of the theta in the language of
section 1.1.

This is not necessarily a show-stopper, since given a draw from the
regular model parameters I could simulate a discrete outcome. However,
shoe-horning that in to Stan might be awkward.

More generally, any assessment of how suitable Stan would be for this
task would be great.  Some earlier discussion refers to Stan as being
very slow for the multinomial, but it looks as if the promised
multinomial_log function has since been implemented (section 33.1).

Background: we have data with a lot of missing values, at all
measurement levels, and marked clustering and are trying to impute. I
have been extending the mice package for R to handle some of the cases
(mlprobit branch of https://github.com/RossBoylan/mice).  The general
framework is a Gibbs sampler for variables to be imputed; this implies
that any particular imputation will be working with complete data
(except for the variable to be imputed).  The task is to create inner
samplers for certain types of variables.

I've implemented models for clustered binary; the first cut was
painfully slow because of high auto-correlation, and so I tried a Hybrid
MC which was somewhat better, though not dramatically so.  I spent some
time tuning it, though probably it could be tuned further.

The alternatives I'm currently contemplating are
1) extend the first cut clustered binary model, based on work by Albert
and Chib, to multinomial outcomes as they suggest.  The drawback is that
the performance was bad for a 2-level variable, suggesting it will be
worse for >2.
2) Use a hybrid MC approach by hand.  Theoretically, this will probably
require a different framework (likely mulitnomial logit) since simple
extension of the current method requires high dimensional integrals of
the normal distribution.  Practically, calculating derivatives was
time-consuming and error-prone (for me) in the binary case, and the
chance of doing it incorrectly for multinomial seems too high.
3) Create a bunch of dummy variables for each categorical outcome,
predict them separately, and then use the highest predicted probability
to give the imputed value (or maybe it would be better to normalize the
probabilities and draw randomly?).
4) Use Stan.

Comments welcome.

On Thursday, August 1, 2013 7:40:33 PM UTC-4, Ross Boylan wrote:
> More generally, any assessment of how suitable Stan would be for this
> task would be great.

I would say that Stan, for the foreseeable future, is ill-suited for any missing data problem, except the one (possibly your case) where only the outcome variable has missingness. In that one case, Stan is decent.

For a nominal outcome, I guess the first thing to consider is whether it is reasonable to consider the missing values to be an additional category. In that case, there is no missing data problem.

Failing that, you probably want to introduce an unknown simplex parameter for each missing outcome. For observed data, the vector of probabilities goes into the likelihood as a function of covariates. For missing data, this function of covariates essentially constitutes a prior on the unknown vector of probabilities. In which case, given the posterior distribution of the unknown probability vectors, you can draw imputations in the generated quantity block from a categorical distribution.

In short, as with all things Stan, if you can write down a joint posterior distribution for all the continuous unknowns, then it is straightforward to use Stan and it will probably work well. That is really a different question than the one asked with Gibbs samplers for missing data where you need a full-conditional distribution for each unknown.

Ben

> Hi, everyone.  I have a relatively well-defned initial question, and then some progressively broader issues.
>
> The manual says "Stan 1.0 does not do discrete sampling."  I'm trying to figure out the implications of that for using
> Stan to do imputation of multinomial outcomes with hierarchical models.  I think it means that Stan will not allow a
> discrete variable to be among the values whose distribution it estimates, i.e., one of the theta in the language of
> section 1.1.

That's right.

> This is not necessarily a show-stopper, since given a draw from the regular model parameters I could simulate a discrete
> outcome. However, shoe-horning that in to Stan might be awkward.

Awkward is putting it kindly.  A better approach is to marginalize out
what you can, but it's hard to do in anything other than simple mixture
models.

> More generally, any assessment of how suitable Stan would be for this task would be great.  Some earlier discussion
> refers to Stan as being very slow for the multinomial, but it looks as if the promised multinomial_log function has
> since been implemented (section 33.1).

I think that's just the usual multinomial on the log
probability scale --- that's the convention in the manual,
which we're going to try to explain better in the 2.0
manual because it's confusing as is.

Stan 2.0 will have a multinomial_logit, for multinomial
logistic regression, with

    multinomial_logit(y|alpha) = multinomial(y|softmax(alpha))

The form on the right is much faster in 2.0, and the customized
one on the left is even faster.  softmax() and multinomial_logit
now have analytic partials instead of using auto-diff internally.

> Background: we have data with a lot of missing values, at all measurement levels, and marked clustering and are trying
> to impute. I have been extending the mice package for R to handle some of the cases (mlprobit branch of
> https://github.com/RossBoylan/mice).  The general framework is a Gibbs sampler for variables to be imputed; this implies
> that any particular imputation will be working with complete data (except for the variable to be imputed).  The task is
> to create inner samplers for certain types of variables.

This sounds like what Andrew and Jennifer and most recently Ben have worked
on in the mi package.  As Ben said, Stan's not a good choice for this.
You couldn't even hack it up well in C++ because of the data immutability
in a Stan model.

> I've implemented models for clustered binary; the first cut was painfully slow because of high auto-correlation, and so
> I tried a Hybrid MC which was somewhat better, though not dramatically so.  I spent some time tuning it, though probably
> it could be tuned further.

NUTS is pretty good for tuning.  Also, did you
tune a diagonal mass matrix for HMC?

> The alternatives I'm currently contemplating are
> 1) extend the first cut clustered binary model, based on work by Albert and Chib, to multinomial outcomes as they
> suggest.  The drawback is that the performance was bad for a 2-level variable, suggesting it will be worse for >2.

Performance as in speed?  Speed goes up with number of outcomes
because of the need to normalize.

> 2) Use a hybrid MC approach by hand.  Theoretically, this will probably require a different framework (likely
> mulitnomial logit) since simple extension of the current method requires high dimensional integrals of the normal
> distribution.  Practically, calculating derivatives was time-consuming and error-prone (for me) in the binary case, and
> the chance of doing it incorrectly for multinomial seems too high.

They're all coded and tested vs. auto-diff in Stan, but that's
C++.

> 3) Create a bunch of dummy variables for each categorical outcome, predict them separately, and then use the highest
> predicted probability to give the imputed value (or maybe it would be better to normalize the probabilities and draw
> randomly?).

> 4) Use Stan.

You could use Stan for various pieces of the above plans, but it's
not going to solve the problem for you out of the box, or even
on its own.

Or you could write a big joint model and use Stan.  It's still
ugly syntactically, but the manual shows you how to do the same
kind of joint modeling approach to missing data you get with BUGS.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Using "block" operator in matrices
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Using "block" operator in matrices
messages.body_plain:
I'm afraid we don't allow block operations
on the left-hand side of assignments.  It's on the
to-do list, but not supported yet.  So the only thing
you can do is a loop.

Sorry the error message is so cryptic.  There's already
an issue filed about it and I hope to fix it before
releasing 2.0.

- Bob

P.S.  The problem is that when the parser reads this line:

    block(A,k,1,1,(k-1))    <- block(B,1,index,1,(index+k-2));

it can't parse it as an assignment, because only variables
with indices are allowed on the LHS of an assignment.  So it
tries to parse an expression and gets this far:

   operand 1:   block(A,k,1,1,(k-1))
   operation:   <
   operand 2:   operation: -
                operand:   block(B,1,index,1,(index+k-2))

It then tries to be helpful by telling you that you can't
apply the logical less-than operator to two matrices.
Now calling the < operation "logical_lt" is doubly confusing, because
"logical_lt" is an internal name we shouldn't be reporting back
to users.  (There's a similar issue some of the indexing
messages, which report on an internal representation of getters.)

That's what I meant by using Stan for part of the

Stan program, but you can implement the HMC parts in

> I think that will be more generalizable and reliable (and possibly faster) than rolling it yourself.

Almost certainly.  Though with tight coding in C++ and
analytical derivatives you should be able to build something
faster than Stan.  There's a price for the generality.

It is a tricky algorithm that's very sensitive to
tuning params.

> I'm afraid we don't allow block operations

>
> Sorry the error message is so cryptic.  There's already

>
> P.S.  The problem is that when the parser reads this line:
>
>     block(A,k,1,1,(k-1))    <- block(B,1,index,1,(index+k-2));
>
> it can't parse it as an assignment, because only variables
> with indices are allowed on the LHS of an assignment.  So it
> tries to parse an expression and gets this far:
>

>    operation:   <
>    operand 2:   operation: -

>
> It then tries to be helpful by telling you that you can't
> apply the logical less-than operator to two matrices.
> Now calling the < operation "logical_lt" is doubly confusing, because
> "logical_lt" is an internal name we shouldn't be reporting back
> to users.  (There's a similar issue some of the indexing

messages.body_plain:
On Friday, August 2, 2013 9:35:49 AM UTC-4, Greg McAvoy wrote:
> I have a time varying, factor analysis model with a shrinkage parameter that I am estimating.  The model that I have runs, but is very slow.  Any thoughts about how to speed it up?

One thing is to not have sampling statements (with the ~) inside a loop with the current version of Stan. Instead, you want to make a temporary mean vector, fill that in a loop, and do one sampling statement outside the loop. This is talked about in the FAQ

https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/4gv3fNCqSNk/J6ZItL2ZJ-IJ

But it looks like you have used the wrong parameterization for the normal distribution. In Stan, the second parameter is the standard deviation. In BUGS, it is the precision (inverse of the variance). In other words, you have a lot of unnecessary pow(*, -2) calls, although that affects the interpretation a lot more than the speed.

Ben

> Stan.

OK.  Thinking about it.

Just to indicate why I was leaning to HMC without Stan:
General:
Adding technology to a late project often makes it later, and certainly
makes it more complex.
To use it I have to learn it.
It might turn out to be unsuitable (in either the "won't do what I want
at all" sense or  the "slow" sense).
[The upshot of the discussion seems to be Stan is suitable in the "will
do that" sense for my intended use,
which is doing an estimate of one particular model within a larger Gibbs
sampler.]

Specific:
The dependence on the compiler brings installation issues, esp. since
some of my work is on Windows.
My intended use is at least a bit off the standard usage pattern.

The good news is that the data Stan would get is complete, since all
imputed values would be filled in, including those for the outcome
variable.  In a perfect world those values would be adjusted within each
iteration of the markov chain (that is, the inner chain for a particular
outcome, the part Stan might do, not the outer Gibbs sampler driving the
overall imputation), but I've already given that up by using the
HybridMC package.

>
>> I think that will be more generalizable and reliable (and possibly
>> faster) than rolling it yourself.

I'm not redoing everything from scratch since I'm using the HybridMC
package.

>
> Almost certainly.  Though with tight coding in C++ and
> analytical derivatives you should be able to build something
> faster than Stan.  There's a price for the generality.
>
> - Bob
>

The alternative I'm using is pure R, though with analytic derivatives.

Also, an earlier remark got completely garbled.  It was

> I was a bit suprised the scale differences cause a complete failure of the
> algorithm; I worried that

That should have been "I was a bit surprised the scale differences did
not cause a complete failure of the
algorithm; I worried that they would."  My concern was that a step size
small enough to match the parameter with the least variation would be
too small to overcome the correlations in the other parameters,  while a
step large enough for those parameters would take the "small" parameters
way out of their plausible range, leading to rejection of the entire
move by the Metropolis phase of the algorithm.

Thanks, Bob, for the pointers about mass.  I see Stan can find good
values automatically, which is certainly a plus.

Ross

messages.body_plain:
Dear group,

i'm trying to run the "Eight schools" example on a cluster computer using Rmpi (before i start with my code). My problem is that the stan code is apparently compiled on each node in the /tmp but this is limited to 100Mo and then it crashes. So I would like to define the path where the code should be compiled. I've tried using save_dso=FALSE but it didn't work. Is there a way to define the path where to compile the code?

Thanks!

Sylvain

R script (try_rstan.R):
library(rstan)
library(foreach)
cl <- makeCluster()
print(clusterCall(cl, function() Sys.info()))

schools_code <- '
  data {
    int<lower=0> J; // number of schools
    real y[J]; // estimated treatment effects
    real<lower=0> sigma[J]; // s.e. of effect estimates
  }
  parameters {
    real mu;
    real<lower=0> tau;
    real eta[J];
  }
  transformed parameters {
    real theta[J];
      for (j in 1:J)
      theta[j] <- mu + tau * eta[j];
    }
  model {
    eta ~ normal(0, 1);
    y ~ normal(theta, sigma);
  }
'

schools_dat <- list(J = 8,
y = c(28, 8, -3, 7, -1, 1, 18, 12),
sigma = c(15, 10, 16, 11, 9, 11, 10, 18))

a <- foreach(i=1:16) %dopar% {
library(rstan)
fit <- stan(model_code = schools_code, data = schools_dat, save_dso = FALSE,iter = 1000, chains = 4) #doesn't work for save_dso = TRUE neither...

save(fit, file=paste("try",i,".Rdata", sep=""))
}

stopCluster(cl)

module load intel-mpi/4.0.0.028 <http://4.0.0.028>

messages.body_plain:
The underlying compiling c++ code is done by package inline, so where the file is created is not configurable by rstan itself.  The save_dso is option is for saving the binary object using R's raw object so it can be saved by R's save/load mechanism.

However, I think package inline using tempfile() to create those temporary files.  So if we change the returned value of function tempdir(), it can be somehow changed.   Checking out the help of tempdir(), one way worth trying is to set an environment variable TMPDIR that points to a writable directory *before* starting R.

--
Jiqiang

On Saturday, August 3, 2013 11:14:19 AM UTC-4, Ross Boylan wrote:
> OK, so I'm thinking of trying stan, and thinking of packaging it for
> Debian.  Any tips?

I think Debian policy would dictate that libstan (the library) be packaged separately from r-noncran-rstan (the R package). I don't think this would be too hard but would require some doing. In particular, the R package would have to patched a bit to use external libraries. I could help. I've used Debian unstable for ages but never gotten involved in packaging anything. Are you a DD?

> In particular, has the external code in libs got any local
> modifications?

No.

> Are there any notable version dependicies?

Short answer no; long answer yes. For Eigen, every release in the 3.x series should work including the one currently in Debian unstable, which is the same one that is embedded with the develop branch of Stan on github. We don't know how far back you can go with Boost but 1.54 is available in the Debian repositories and is embedded with Stan.

Bob is really adverse to supporting older releases of the libraries (or for that matter older versions of the C++ compiler, but we should be okay with any g++ or clang++ in testing or unstable). So, officially Stan only supports the versions of the dependencies that it embeds, and it would be up to the Debian maintainer(s) to patch around that for alternative versions of the dependencies if the need arises, which it shouldn't for the moment.

>  Debian
> packages generally rely on existing Debian packages for external libraries.

Right, there is also gtest but that almost never gets updated and is only necessary for the unit tests so it could be merely suggested.

> Also, what's up with the recursive rstan directories
> https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/tree/develop/rstan/rstan?

It isn't essential to anything.

> I think the binary packages that would result include one for the stan
> library, one for the stan executable, and one for the r package.

Yeah, technically there is no stan executable, but there is a stanc binary that parses the .stan files. And then the patched R package would need to depend on libstan and stanc.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
On 8/3/13 11:14 AM, Ross Boylan wrote:
> OK, so I'm thinking of trying stan, and thinking of packaging it for
> Debian.  Any tips?
>
> In particular, has the external code in libs got any local
> modifications?

No.  RStan doesn't include all of Boost, but the regular
Stan distribution does.

 > Are there any notable version dependicies?

We only test the latest versions of the libs, which we distribute
with Stan and RStan.  I don't recall any dependencies, but having said that,
Boost and Eigen and Stan have all changed considerably over the last two years
of development.  We'd love to hear back about compatibility issues --- we just
don't have the resources to test all combinations of compiler, lib and platform.
So we restrict ourselves to relatively recent g++ and clang++ and mingw,
the most recent versions of the libs, Mac OS latest, Windows 7, and various versions
of Linux our developers use.

> Debian
> packages generally rely on existing Debian packages for external libraries.

That's typical for linux, but you can always use other versions of
the libs.   Stan is very easy to customize for the location of the
libs.  It assumes they're where they are in the Stan distribution, so
you'd have to use the right set of properties for the makefile to have
them point elsewhere.

> Also, what's up with the recursive rstan directories
> https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/tree/develop/rstan/rstan?

I'm guessing that is just mirroring the R distribution structure,
but you'll have to ask the R wizards.

> I think the binary packages that would result include one for the stan
> library, one for the stan executable, and one for the r package.

Right --- there's the library archive libstan.a, the Stan-to-C++ translator bin/stanc,
and then the R package.

The major issue with packaging Stan itself is that it
needs a C++ compiler to compile the models.

- Bob

The point is not whether it's easy to use different lib versions. The
difference is that debian maintainers will look very suspiciously at
any new package that bundles a nonstandard lib version rather than
using the system one. It's a principle which helps the debian
maintaners ensure that bugfixes and security issues can be handled
coherently. (Imagine if they had to patch a security issue in boost,
and they had dozens of different versions of boost in the repo which
they had to individually check and patch.)

I've had trouble with this while packaging some other software. I
think you'll find that if you can make "stan.deb" use system
libraries, the debian admins will be much much happier with it and the
flow to getting it available will be much smoother.

> needs a C++ compiler to compile the models.

That's no problem - just a runtime dependency declared in the debian
control file, which ensures one of the appropriate compilers is
available.

Dan

Also, it would re-open the possibility of getting Stan-related packages onto CRAN.

> How does it facilitate Python integration?  (I'm pretty much
> completely ignorant about Python and Linux packaging.)

The Pystan repo is like RStan in that it embeds its dependencies. If there were Stan-related Debian packages, then it would be pretty easy to make a tiny python-pystan Debian package that also used the system libraries. It doesn't make anything easier on Mac or Windows.

> > It just means doing a lot of things the
> > Debian way instead of the wrong way.
>

> lib and compiler dependencies.

Debian is as much a religion as it is a Linux distribution. But I would say that three of the packaging principles are

-- Don't embed dependencies on other software
-- Make version requirements as lenient as possible
-- Separate the library from the headers from the binaries from the test-suite, etc.

(R)Stan is pretty much the opposite of that, but it wouldn't be that hard to have a Debian git branch that facilitated doing things the way Debian requires them.

Ben

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] packaging Stan for Debian
messages.body_plain:
I'll try to respond to some of the issues that have been raised.

I'm not a debian developer, but I have discussed this on debian-science
(and just now r-sig-debian) and there seem to be people there who could
do a sponsored upload and perhaps help in other ways.

Why not try just installing the thing?  I might, but it makes me a
little nervous.  Debian has a nice way of managing things, and stomping
on it can have unfortunate effects.  For example, I don't particularly
want to have multiple versions of libraries like boost and eigen on my
system, and if the installer touched areas that are supposed to be under
management of the package system it would be a bad thing (e.g.,
installing stuff to /usr or /lib--/usr/local is OK).  Worst case would
be if make install overwrite some libraries that are part of debian
package and made random other software that uses the libraries fail.

I figure if I go as far as rearranging things for myself I might as well
try to make Debian package(s) as a public service.

On the issue of library versions, a few more comments.  Debian is not
just the OS or the low-level stuff, it is supposed to be a coherent set
of packages that work together.  So each release will have its own set
of libraries like boost and eigen (boost is actually packaged in several
different parts and the current stable distribution has libeigen3 and
libeigen2 available).  So the natural way to package stan would be to
declare a debian package dependency on packages containing the necessary
libraries (as well as the g++ compiler, which again varies with the
release).  Ideally this means that people with different versions of the
libraries (e.g., because they are running different releases, or perhaps
running a Debian derivative like Ubuntu) can get the source and build
it, using whatever libraries they have.  Of course, if some version of a
library is absolutely necessary one can declare that, and life becomes
more painful for those who are not at the cutting edge.

All of which underlines how important a good test suite is; I see there
are some tests in the R package and Ben mentioned gtest and unit tests
for the main program.  Does gtest run the unit tests, or is it a program
that is used by (some of?) the unit tests.

Bob remarked, on the subject of supporting older versions of the libs
(and perhaps of g++):

> I just don't think it should be a priority given everything
> else we have going on and how easy it is to use the most
> recent libs on all platforms.
>

I don't disagree about the priorities, but using the most recent libs is not easy
on most linux distributions.  The distribution (which in this context means not
just Debian but a particular release, e.g. Debian wheezy) will come with a particular version
of the tools/libraries and using a later one will not be straightforward for many
users.  Attempting to install a later version improperly could destabilize the system.
Debian has versions that are more current and less stable; in order of
increasing currentness and decreasing reliability they are testing, unstable, and
experimental (that latter is not a full distribution and the former are essentially pre-releases).
It also has backports of more recent versions of some packages to the current stable system.  In particular
there are backports of R available through cran, though not the usual backports locations.

So an informed user can do anything, but it's not necessarily straightforward.
And some people stick with the official releases, aka stable, because it is more
stable and has better support (including security fixes).

Debian provides a way of specifying tests that are optionally run at the
time the package is built; we could hook available tests into that
mechanism.  That would make it easy to build and test the packages on
all the Debian architectures.

With the R package I guess there's a tension between wanting to provide
a nearly "one-click" install experience and providing a regular R
library.  Definitely for Debian the r-noncran-stan package would be
basically rstan without the included stan subproject.

Apparently stan has a static library, libstan.a.  I think Debian policy
favors using dynamic libraries; is there any particular reason for the
static form?

Ross

Our tests take on the order of hours to run if you run the model

we can rely on).

Not that I know of.  I don't know how to build non-static ones, but
someone on the team can probably figure it out. We use R's build tools and
the inline package to build dynamically linkable versions of the models for R.

- Bob

I think the static libraries provide more reliable control over the
libraries linked to. With dynamic libraries the libraries chosen are
deliberately deferred until execution time, which increases the risk of
picking up the "wrong" version of the library (e.g., the system version
of a library, rather than the one shipped with stan).

These issues are probably mostly irrelevant to boost and eigen, which
are primarily compile time header libraries (though of course their are
analogous issues gettting the right include file).  Some boost
components have small run-time libraries they rely on.

I've also read reports that static libraries run faster.

Ross

messages.subject: Combining information
messages.subject_clean: Combining information
messages.body_plain:
Dear STAN-users,

Suppose I have 3 dummy variables, indicating whether a survey respondent living in area i smokes, drinks, and exercises. To estimate the (within-area) joint distribution of these variables, I model the survey data as:

n[i,1:K] ~ dmulti( phi[i,1:K] , N[i] )
phi[i,1:K] ~ dirichlet( [1,..,1] )   or:   phi[i,1:K] ~ logisticNormal( [mu[],sigma[] )

where 1:K represents the 2^3 combinations of the dummy variables. Because the survey data is relatively sparse, I want to combine the estimation of phi with additional information about the marginal distribution of each risk factor. Suppose I can model the marginal distribution of each risk factor as:

logit( prob_smoking[i] ) <- inprod( b1[],X1[i,] )
logit( prob_drinking[i] ) <- inprod( b2[],X2[i,] )
logit( prob_exercising[i] ) <- inprod( b3[],X3[i,] ) ,

does it make sense (and is it possible?) to combine the two sources of information, e.g. by specifying something like this in STAN:

sum( phi[i,1:K] .* [0 0 0 0 1 1 1 1] ) <- inv_logit( b1*X1) )
sum( phi[i,1:K] .* [0 0 1 1 0 0 1 1] ) <- inv_logit( b2*X2) )
sum( phi[i,1:K] .* [0 1 0 1 0 1 0 1] ) <- inv_logit( b3*X3) )

where the sum of the elements of phi is equal to the prob_smoking, prob_drinking, and prob_exercising?

Thanks!
Marcel

On Saturday, August 3, 2013 8:15:13 PM UTC-4, Ross Boylan wrote:

As much as I would like Debian packages to be available, you can easily get it working yourself on a Debian system where the only cost is a lot of wasted disk space. I have about 4 copies of Boost, which is crazy, but doesn't really hurt anything.

All that said, making Debian packages would be conceptually simple. It would just be

Patch the makefile to replace these lines
EIGEN ?= lib/eigen_3.2.0
BOOST ?= lib/boost_1.54.0
GTEST ?= lib/gtest_1.6.0
with the Debian equivalents
EIGEN ?= /usr/include/eigen3/
BOOST ?= /usr/include
GTEST ?= /usr/include
(or better to use pkg-config) and delete everything under lib/
For the libstan package, make bin/libstan.a and mv it to /usr/lib/stan/bin
For the libstanc package, make bin/libstanc.a and mv it to /usr/lib/stan/bin
For the stanc package, make bin/stanc and mv it to /usr/bin
For the stan_print package, make bin/print and mv it to /usr/bin/stan_print. Replace any calls in stan to bin/print with /usr/bin/stan_print.
For the libstan package, mv src/stan to /usr/include/stan
For the libstan package, mv src/docs to /usr/share/stan/docs and mv src/models to /usr/share/stan/models

I'm not quite sure what to do with the unit tests under src/test but they should go somewhere. The tricky part is that some of the unit tests depend on stanc while the libstan package shouldn't necessarily have a hard dependency on stanc. And that's basically it. The rest is just compliance with Debian policy.

> library.  Definitely for Debian the r-noncran-stan package would be

Doing a r-noncran-rstan package would take more work. We would probably have to utilize autotools.

Not a compelling one as far as I know of.

messages.body_plain:
I do not really understand the question here.  But as we have always put, what Stan does is to specify the log of the posterior density function of continuous parameters and use NUTS (a variant of HMC) to draw samples from the posterior.  However, how to specify the posterior and make sure the correctness are totally up to the user.  So if you can express your idea of combing information into a posterior distribution, Stan can help.  Then the real question is whether you can write down the posterior mathematically.

--
Jiqiang

About the rstan/rstan/rstan directory structure:
rstan is the git project.
rstan/stan is a submodule that imports the stan project
rstan/rstan is for building the rstan tarball.
rstan/rstan/rstan is the actual R library that the upper directory builds.

rstan/rstan/Makefile copies or links stuff from rstan/stan into rstan/rstan/rstan (!).

The problem with using bcp, e.g., in rstan/rstan/makefile, is that this
makes the build system dependent on another external binary.

However, that part of the build system is really the meta-build system (I think):
it is the system that prepares the tarballs that end users will receive.
Since it does not require the end user to have bcp, it might be more acceptable.

> Obviously, that wouldn't fly in Debian, which is why I mentioned
> that instead of depending on libboost1.54-all, we would have to depend on
> the particular parts of Boost that Stan uses, which differs depending on
> whether we are talking about the stanc package or the libstan package.

Actually, the headers of boost all seem to be in a single package.  It is the the little
boost binary libraries that are in separate packages.

The Debian way would be to remove the external libraries from the  (Debian) source package
entirely and simply have the package depend, or build-depend, on the appropriate
libraries.

The current packaging is inconsistent on handling of external
dependencies.  To get things working one needs a compiler, R (at leat
for rstan), boost, eigen and (sometimes?) gtest.  The first 2 are left
as an exercise for the user, while the remainder are provided.

Ross

As Jiqiang points out, this is more of a stats question than
a Stan question.  I didn't understand the R notation.

Might it make sense in this case to define three boolean variables for smoking,
drinking and exercising, say y[1], y[2] and y[3] and then model y jointly in
a multivariate regression?   The simplest thing to do would be the logistic
version of:

    http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seemingly_unrelated_regressions

where you have separate regressions for the expectation of each variable, but
the errors are tied in a multivariate structure to allow correlations.

I don't actually know if anybody uses this.  Is there a section in Andrew
and Jennifer's book on multiple output regression like this?  (I don't recall
one.)

- Bob

We don't yet support ragged arrays.  There are a few
workarounds described in the manual (see for example the
LDA model and the missing data examples).  The typical way
is to just use something like a data-frame representation
in R.  For instance, if you want a ragged 2D array, you
can use three parallel arrays for row ID, column ID,
and value.  For instance,

    row,col,val
    1,2,5,
    1,3,7
    2,2,6

indicates m[1,2] = 5, m[1,3] = 7, and so on.

This gives you all the indexing you need, but we don't
support any sparse matrix ops.

- Bob

Nothing's mandatory in terms of form.  As Daniel pointed out,
your issue was with the scope of the variable n.  Stan scoping
in terms of loop variables works like in progamming languages
like Python and C++.  (R's scoping is very odd, but your example
wouldn't have worked there, either.)

> Btw, I didn't find in the manual an example doing multiple equation models by hand or using matrices, as Bob mentioned

>
>
> By relaxing such assumption you mean considering the possibility of correlation between disturbances in both equations
> (e.g. such as in a SUR model)? Is there any example on how to implement such a thing with the bivariate normal
> distribution parameterized with covariance matrix in Stan?

The SUR gives you covariance on the errors in a bunch of "seemingly
unrelated" regressions.  I'm not sure how to set that up in your case where
there's an explicit dependence between y[n,1] and y[n,2].  For the normal,
I'm always surprised what you can do analytically...

Plain old SUR if  you have predictors x[n] would be

    y[n] ~ multi_normal(x[n] * beta, Sigma);

where

    y[n] is a K-vector of outcomes

    x[n] is a D-vector of predictors

    beta is a D x K matrix of regression coefficients

    Sigma is a K x K covariance matrix

We haven't vectorized multi_normal yet, but eventually this'll
just be y ~ multi_normal(x * beta, Sigma).

In hierarchical models, you can also put a covariance prior
on your regression coefficients.

I need to add sections on both of these to the manual.  Soon,
we'll have all the regression models from Gelman and Hill's
regression book implemented (they do the hierarchical priors,
but I don't recall SUR).

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Other names for this problem are "sampling from a convex polytope" or "sampling from the solution space of a linear programming problem". The mathematical definition is sampling uniformly from the set {x | Ax = b, x>0}, or sampling from the set of solutions of Ax = b, for some matrix A and vector b, where all the components of x are positive, assuming a bounded space.

I have implemented a hit-and-run sampler for the problem, it is located at https://github.com/davidkane9/kmatching. However, when running the Gelman-Rubin diagnostic on multiple chains, it becomes clear that we would need to run an impractical number of samples in order to converge to a stationary distribution.

Have there ever been problems of the same nature solved by RStan, if so, what specific functions should I look at?

Attached is a problem statement.

>From a statistical perspective, perfect knowledge of the variables b is a bit presumptuous.  A more robust model allows measurement noise,

b ~ normal(A * x, sigma);

If A is known, then x and sigma can easily be inferred in Stan.  Positivity constrains on both are easily included in their definitions,

real<lower=0> x;
real<lower=0> sigma;

Additional constraints on x, such as a known sum, can be incorporated in the prior (for example, making the x a simplex and using a Dirichlet prior).

It's also straightforward to generalize when A is not known exactly by making it a parameter rather than data (I had great success in problems like this where A is a transfer matrix: model each column of A as a simplex with a Dirichlet prior and use any existing data to build a posterior for the columns that gets used as a prior for the joint inference).

On 8/8/13 10:59 AM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Thursday, August 8, 2013 10:48:39 AM UTC-4, Martin Šmíra wrote:
>
>     1)  I'm trying to find out if Stan has an alternative tool to WinBugs WBDev, where I could define my own function
>     and then just call it in a model specification?
>
>
> No, although that has been mentioned. Most of the time, it is usually enough to manipulate the lp__ symbol for Stan <=
> 1.3.0; the syntax is changing for stan >= 2.0.

Basically, what used to be written as:

    lp__ <- lp__ + y;

will be written as:

    increment_log_prob(y);

The reason was to cut down on user errors for forgetting
to increment.  You can use this to implement just about any density,
though Stan's lack of good debugging and compiler tools makes it
a challenge to implement anything too difficult (HMMs and Gaussian
processes are about as far as I've gone within Stan).

You can also pretty easily link in templated C++ definitions,
though there's not an easy extension mechanism besides rebuilding
Stan at the moment.  We will be adding that soon so that you can
dynamically link in new functions defined externally to Stan's own
code.

>     2)  How long do you estimate that it'll take to implement sampling of discrete parameters?  The thing is that I'm
>     writing some model excercises for newcomers to Bayesian and I want to keep the models simple.
>
>
> poisson(1000)

Unit free estimates, to boot :-)

We're thinking about discrete sampling, but don't have a concrete
plan or time frame yet.  And unless we have some conceptual breakthroughs,
it will likely be a bit clunky and redundant even when we do add it.

>     3)  What is the difference between function abs() and fabs(). In the manual its described the same. But my model was
>     returning wierd outputs till I've added the "f" in front of all abs.
>
>
> This may have been harmonized for the next version of Stan. fabs() is for floating-point numbers.

It's all about the signatures, and particularly the return types:

    int abs(int);

and

    real fabs(real);

Because int can be promoted to real, the second can also be used as:

    real fabs(int);

So the f vs. no-f controls the type of the result.

You see the same thing with fmax and max, where there's further subtlety
due to multiple arguments.

- Bob

> I am trying to implement the LKJ approach to estimate the mean vector and covariance matrix from a multivariate normal distribution. My understanding of the approach is basic, and I have mostly pieced it together from the STAN mailing lists. Any help would be appreciated.

We regret having the lkj_cov density because it hard-codes a lognormal prior on the standard deviations. It is better to just put a lkj_corr prior on the correlation matrix and whatever prior you want on the standard deviations. But to answer your questions directly

> QUESTION 1.
> The code runs, and I obtain reasonable estimates, however I get the following error
> > > Informational Message: The parameter state is about to be Metropolis rejected due to the following underlying, non-fatal (really) issue (and please ignore that what comes next might say 'error'): Error in function stan::prob::lkj_cov_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Covariance matrix is 1.#INF:0, but must be finite!
> > > If the problem persists across multiple draws, you might have a problem with an initial state or a gradient somewhere.
> > > If the problem does not persist, the resulting samples will still be drawn from the posterior.

If it just happens a small number of times toward the beginning, don't worry about it. Overflow happens and if so, proposals get rejected. Not a big deal.

> My prior on the standard deviation seems reasonable, and eta is 1... so I am not sure why I am getting this error. Is my parameterization incorrect?

It's fine.

> QUESTION 2.
>  Are there any guidelines on how to choose the value of eta?

The manual has some explanation. Basically, eta is akin to the shape parameter of a beta distribution if both shape parameters are constrained to be equal (especially in the 2x2 case where there is only 1 free parameter in the correlation matrix). So

0 < eta < 1 -> U-shaped (i.e. correlation matrix has no mode)
eta == 1 -> uniform over the space of correlation matrices
1 < eta -> upside down U-shaped (i.e. correlation matrix as a mode at the identity)
As eta approaches infinity, the only correlation matrix with positive density is the identity.

Ben

On 8/9/13 3:54 AM, Sergio Polini wrote:
> I attach a few suggestions about Ch5. The main changes are:
>
> 1. �5.1-5.7
>
> I've centered the variables even when not required by the model in order to improve both speed and effective sample
> size.

Do we want to do this or have the model examples follow
the text?

> As far as I can understand, this happens because centering reduces posterior correlation of the parameters.

Linear transformation like centering and scaling won't
affect correlation.  But they will affect the intercept,
which has to absorb the slack from offsets.  Look
at what happens to predictors under centering:

    alpha * x[i] + beta

    == alpha * (x[i] - mean(x)) + (beta + alpha * mean(x))

The coefficient is the same, but the new intercept is offset
by alpha * mean(x).

> Parameter values are recovered in the generated quantities block.
> However:
> -- I don't know if standardization would be better (I did not try);

If the variables have different scales, then yes.  We do adaptation,
but it's approximate and it's faster to just start with everything on the
same unit scale.  This does affect the meaning of the priors, though.

> -- I can't understand why the effective sample size gets larger for parameters but smaller for lp__.

We don't really care about ESS for lp__ so much.  It's a
non-linear function of the parameters (the log probability
function to be exact).

>
> I've generated the predicted (fitted) values in the generated quantities block.

> *5) * If I want truncated distribution, is it enough to just declare it in parameter declaration or should I put also

> eg. T[0,] behind sampling statement?  Or both? Is there any difference? Isn't it useless to use T[] ?

Constraints in the parameter declarations leave the distribution
uniform over the constrained space.  If the truncation is needed in
the log density, you need to include it.  In general:

     Foo(y|theta) T[L,H] = log Foo(y|theta) / (FooCDF(H|theta) - FooCDF(L|theta))

So if any of L, H or theta depends on a parameter, you need it.

There's nothing fundamentally wrong with the model specification
I can see.  There are a couple of challenging pieces of it.

First is the explicit latent overdispersed binomial.

Second is the challenge of identifying parameters in this setup:

parameters {
   real<lower=0,upper=10> sigmaalpha;
   real<lower=0> delta;
...
}
transformed parameters{
   real<lower=0> mualpha;
   mualpha <- delta * sigmaalpha;
...
model {
   sigmaalpha ~ uniform(0,10);
   delta ~ normal(0,1)T[0,];
...
   alpha ~ normal(mualpha,sigmaalpha);
...

The only identification comes from the normal(0,1) on delta, which will tend to
drive it as small as possible.  Does sigmaalpha hover around the boundary at 10?

You can also make the model more efficient using logit instead
of probit (the link function is computationally simpler).  And you
could apply the Matt trick to the hierarchical parameters, which should
also help.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Definitions potentially useful to relate Stan output to frequentists properties of models
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Definitions potentially useful to relate Stan output to frequentists properties of models
messages.body_plain:
This is probably not the best place to discuss relations
between frequentist and Bayesian stats that isn't Stan specific.

Stan's samplers let you sample from any distribution for
which you can write the log probability function.  So you
can use that for some types of frequentist analysis.

Stan also lets you derive frequentist estimates using
optimization (MLE or penalized MLE).  But we don't have
any hypothesis testing or confidence interval estimation
in place for the estimates.

- Bob

average of parameter samples over the traceplot.  It's on the same scale.
I'd restrict it to after warmup, because then the value represents the
estimated mean if sampling had stopped at that iteration.

On the one hand, it would be nice to have Stan satisfy all of
our user's requirements --- if we don't have these things, people will
still need to use Coda, etc., if they need them.  On the other
hand, we want to encourage what we think are good practices.

messages.body_plain:
Unlike BUGS, Stan does not have a way to represent R's NA (undefined/missing)
values.  So you can't provide them as part of input in RStan and therefore
can't directly translate BUGS-style missing-data models.   There's a chapter
of the manual on coding missing-data models in Stan.  It requires preprocessing
the data into a different format and also fiddling with the model.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Sorry -- I should've looked at the model more closely.

The error you're seeing arises when a local or transformed
variable is not properly initialized or when data is initialized
as NaN.  Parameters are always initialized, so you don't need to
worry about them.  So the problem has to be xobserved, because it's
the only non-parameter implicated:

 > xobserved[study, subject,1] ~ multi_normal(musubject[study, subject], D[study]);

It must be xobserved because everything else is a parameter.
This definition is suspicious because it might not initialize
all of xobserved depending on the values of grav_ind[b].

 >     for (b in 1:nRowGrav) xobserved[grav_ind[b,1],grav_ind[b,2],grav_ind[b,3],2] <- gravlongx[b];

You can try printing it before you use it to debug where this
is happening.

- Bob

Dear Bob,

I just picked up where I left of in March, hoping that some of the issues of earlier versions of STAN have been resolved. Justed wanted to notify you that in the current version of rstan (1.3.0), truncation and vectorization of the lognormal distribution do work, but not when used at the same time:

TRANSLATING MODEL 'Coffeng2013Malaria' FROM Stan CODE TO C++ CODE NOW.
Error in stanc(file = file, model_code = model_code, model_name = model_name,  :
  failed to parse Stan model 'Coffeng2013Malaria' with error message:
EXPECTATION FAILURE LOCATION: file=input; line=70, column=3

  t1 ~ lognormal(log_T1,S_T1) T[5,12];

  ^-- here

DIAGNOSTIC(S) FROM PARSER:
no matches for function name="lognormal_cdf"
    arg 0 type=real[1]
    arg 1 type=real
    arg 2 type=real

available function signatures for lognormal_cdf:
0.  lognormal_cdf(real, real, real) : real

lower bound in truncation type does not match sampled variate in distribution's type
Parser expecting: "}"

t1 is declared in the parameter block as "real<lower=5,upper=12> t1[Nind]" ); log_T1 and S_T1 are parameters with unknown values, hence I need the truncation of the prior for t1 (because of the non-constant values of log_T1 and S_T1). Specifying a loop for each component of t1 solves the issue (though is somewhat slower).

Best,
Luc

Hi,

I thought STAN allowed missing values in the MVN? How do I code these values then?

On Tuesday, August 13, 2013 12:05:15 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>

> > Hi Bob,

> > Thank you for suggesting the print function - I hadn't thought of that!
> >
> > So my code is correctly transforming parameters/data, and the indexes are all working correctly in the likelihood loop.
> > In my data vector for the MVN, occasionally one of the observations will be missing:
> > [1.#QNAN:0,3.5:0]
> > and sometimes both will be missing
> > [1.#QNAN:0,1.#QNAN:0]
> >
> > Do I have to do further processing to get the MVN to work? It seems that the values of my missing observations "#QNAN:0"
> > reflect the error I am getting when I run the model?
>
> Yes, you can't put NaN into multivariate normal because
> it leads to a NaN result in the density.
>
> - Bob
>
>
> > On Sunday, August 11, 2013 1:06:33 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:

> >     Sorry -- I should've looked at the model more closely.

> >     variable is not properly initialized or when data is initialized
> >     as NaN.  Parameters are always initialized, so you don't need to
> >     worry about them.  So the problem has to be xobserved, because it's
> >     the only non-parameter implicated:
> >
> >       > xobserved[study, subject,1] ~ multi_normal(musubject[study, subject], D[study]);
> >
> >     It must be xobserved because everything else is a parameter.
> >     This definition is suspicious because it might not initialize
> >     all of xobserved depending on the values of grav_ind[b].

> >       >     for (b in 1:nRowGrav) xobserved[grav_ind[b,1],grav_ind[b,2],grav_ind[b,3],2] <- gravlongx[b];

> > > >>
> > > >> I've centered the variables even when not required by the model in order to improve both speed and effective sample
> > > >> size.
> > > >
> > > > Do we want to do this or have the model examples follow
> > > > the text?
> > > >
> > > >> As far as I can understand, this happens because centering reduces posterior correlation of the parameters.
> > > >
> > > > Linear transformation like centering and scaling won't
> > > > affect correlation.  But they will affect the intercept,
> > > > which has to absorb the slack from offsets.  Look
> > > > at what happens to predictors under centering:
> > > >
> > > >   alpha * x[i] + beta
> > > >
> > > >   == alpha * (x[i] - mean(x)) + (beta + alpha * mean(x))
> > > >
> > > > The coefficient is the same, but the new intercept is offset
> > > > by alpha * mean(x).

The manual outlines the steps for command-line execution.
You can use RStan to produce appropriate data and init
files.

I believe the next version of RStan will independently allow
the setting of compiler optimization (fast or debug) and
bounds checking for arrays (no-check [fast] or check [slower,safer]).
And be configured out of the box for compiler=fast / bounds=check.
(Naming is hard --- compile time is longer with the "fast" setting
because it's more work to do the optimization.)

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
R's save/load should work and I think it worked here.  However, what are saved are the samples and the compiled model (ie, the dynamic shared object, AKA dynamic link library).  We cannot save/load the model object (which can be understood as an C++ object) that is created using the dynamic shared object.  So you can use the saved stanfit object to resample, but you cannot call some methods such as get_num_upars.

--
Jiqiang

On Thursday, August 15, 2013 12:01:30 PM UTC-4, Brendan wrote:
> I'm trying to set up an Ordered Logit of lifetimes (discrete years, 1,2,...,K). Observational units are 'born' at different times. The data has right censoring; plenty of my observations have yet to 'die', but I know how far they've made it to date.
>
> I've rather verbosely described my failed efforts below, but can anyone think of a sensible way of specifying this kind of model?

Can you explain to us why you are inclined to use an ordered logit model for these data? The ordered logit model estimates unknown cutpoints. In your case (and many situations with survival analysis) you know the cutpoints (when a year changes over) and know that they are equally spaced. So, it would seem that you need a count model, rather than an ordinal one. That is still going to be difficult in Stan due to the difficulties with discrete unknowns but easier than trying to do it with an ordinal model.

Ben

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Missing Data: multivariate normal, how to make it work?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I figured out my problem: missing observations must be declared as a parameter variable, and then assigned to the correct indices of transformed parameter variable in place of observed data. Everything works well now.

On Wednesday, August 14, 2013 10:49:54 AM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I don't know how to make it work for multi-variate normal, but
> others might know.
>
> You can read the chapter on missing data in the manual, but I
> don't have any advice other than that for your particular case.
>
> - Bob
>
>
> On 8/13/13 12:34 PM, Markian Pahuta wrote:
> > Hi,
> > I thought STAN allowed missing values in the MVN? How do I code these values then?
> >
> > On Tuesday, August 13, 2013 12:05:15 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> >
> >
> >     On 8/12/13 10:00 PM, Markian Pahuta wrote:
> >      > Hi Bob,
> >      >
> >      > Thank you for suggesting the print function - I hadn't thought of that!
> >      >
> >      > So my code is correctly transforming parameters/data, and the indexes are all working correctly in the likelihood
> >     loop.
> >      > In my data vector for the MVN, occasionally one of the observations will be missing:
> >      > [1.#QNAN:0,3.5:0]
> >      > and sometimes both will be missing
> >      > [1.#QNAN:0,1.#QNAN:0]
> >      >
> >      > Do I have to do further processing to get the MVN to work? It seems that the values of my missing observations
> >     "#QNAN:0"
> >      > reflect the error I am getting when I run the model?
> >
> >     Yes, you can't put NaN into multivariate normal because
> >     it leads to a NaN result in the density.
> >
> >     - Bob
> >
> >
> >      > On Sunday, August 11, 2013 1:06:33 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> >      >
> >      >     Sorry -- I should've looked at the model more closely.
> >      >
> >      >     The error you're seeing arises when a local or transformed
> >      >     variable is not properly initialized or when data is initialized
> >      >     as NaN.  Parameters are always initialized, so you don't need to
> >      >     worry about them.  So the problem has to be xobserved, because it's
> >      >     the only non-parameter implicated:
> >      >
> >      >       > xobserved[study, subject,1] ~ multi_normal(musubject[study, subject], D[study]);
> >      >
> >      >     It must be xobserved because everything else is a parameter.
> >      >     This definition is suspicious because it might not initialize
> >      >     all of xobserved depending on the values of grav_ind[b].
> >      >
> >      >       >     for (b in 1:nRowGrav) xobserved[grav_ind[b,1],grav_ind[b,2],grav_ind[b,3],2] <- gravlongx[b];
> >      >
> >      >     You can try printing it before you use it to debug where this
> >      >     is happening.
> >      >
> >      >     - Bob
> >      >
> >      >
> >      >
> >      >
> >      >
> >      >     On 8/11/13 11:44 AM, Markian Pahuta wrote:
> >      >      > Hi Bob,
> >      >      >
> >      >      > Thank you for your reply. I am aware of this difference, and used the approach in section 6.4 of the
> >     manual. My
> >      >     input
> >      >      > data format has no NAs.
> >      >      >
> >      >      > Does the error mean that I haven't implemented the transformed parameters correctly?
> >      >      >
> >      >      >
> >      >      > On Sunday, August 11, 2013 11:09:00 AM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> >      >      >
> >      >      >     Unlike BUGS, Stan does not have a way to represent R's NA (undefined/missing)
> >      >      >     values.  So you can't provide them as part of input in RStan and therefore
> >      >      >     can't directly translate BUGS-style missing-data models.   There's a chapter
> >      >      >     of the manual on coding missing-data models in Stan.  It requires preprocessing
> >      >      >     the data into a different format and also fiddling with the model.
> >      >      >
> >      >      >     - Bob
> >      >      >
> >      >      >     On 8/10/13 4:38 PM, Markian Pahuta wrote:
> >      >      >      > Hi,
> >      >      >      >
> >      >      >      > I have written a hierarchical model with a MVN likelihood. I am able to get the model to run when
> >     no data
> >      >     is missing
> >      >      >      > (use file full.dat). But when I run the model with missing data (missing.dat), I get the error:
> >      >      >      >
> >      >      >      >         /Error : Error in function stan::prob::multi_normal_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Random
> >     variable[0]  is
> >      >      >     1.#QNAN:0,
> >      >      >      >         but must not be nan!/
> >      >      >      >
> >      >      >      >         /error occurred during calling the sampler; sampling not done/
> >      >      >      >
> >      >      >      >
> >      >      >      >   The RSTAN model is:
> >      >      >      >
> >      >      >      >     |
> >      >      >      >     library(rstan)
> >      >      >      >
> >      >      >      >     mcode <- '

messages.body_plain:
On 8/20/13 9:56 AM, Brendan wrote:
> Cheers for the quick response Ben!
>
> Point taken with the count data. My main inferential interest is the probability that a new unit 'dies' in the next
> year, so my thought process started with a logit. I'm also trying to build my intuition with Stan ahead of data coming
> in, by trying lots of specifications with synthetic data. So, I'm afraid the answer to your question is 'No' :) .
>
> A Poisson type model with some allowance for overdispersion is a very good idea. I've tried to get at it in a couple of
> ways, the least awful is below.
>
> I took the approach used in Gelman & Hill (p. 382) for overdispersion in BUGS, with Gaussian noise on the linear
> predictor passed to the Poisson distribution function, and the lp__ incrementing method for censored data in the manual
> (p. 45),
>
> |
> model {
>      mu ~ normal(0, 100);
>      beta ~ normal(0, 100);
>
>      for(n in 1:N_obs)
>          lambada_obs[n] ~ normal(mu + x_obs[n] * beta,  sigma);
>
>      y_obs ~ poisson_log(lambada_obs);
>
>      for(n in 1:N_cen)
>          lambada_cen[n] ~ normal(mu + x_cen[n] * beta,  sigma);
>
>      lp__ <- lp__ + N_cen * log1m(poisson_cdf(L, lambada_cen));
> }
>
> |
>
> ...where L (int <lower=0> L[N_cen]) is the lower bounds on the censored data. My intuition is that I should be

> exponentiating the linear predictor before I pass it to the |poisson_cdf|, but Stan doesn't like the ways I've tried,

> and either terminates the R session or throws out of bounds errors.

>
> Confusingly, it seems to estimate mu okay (with enough iterations), but seems to estimate beta and sigma very low. The
> estimate of beta gets lower as the proportion of censored data gets higher, stepping over 2 SDs away from both the
> parameter in the data generating mechanism, and the point estimate from a 'full obs only' model when censoring's ~50% of
> data on a toy problem. When the proportion of censored data is relatively modest (~11%), beta looks okay, but sigma is
> low,  > 2 SDs away from the 'obs only' estimate, and the parameter in the DGM.
>
> So, the specification above performs worse than an 'obs only' model on the same data set.
>
> Any ideas on where I've gone wrong?
>

Shouldn't that last line be:

     for (n in 1:N_cen)
       lp__ <- lp__ + log1m(poisson_cdf(L[n],lambda_cen[n]));

That is, it's the ccdf function you want vectorized.

     log Poisson_CCDF(L,lambda_cen)

     = SUM_n log Poisson_CCDF(L[n],lambda_cen[n])

     = SUM_n log1m(Poisson_CDF(L[n], lambda_cen[n]);

What you have is:

     log(1 - SUM_n log poisson_CDF(L[n], lambda_cen[n]);

- Bob

I'm using rstan with set_cppo("fast"). I'll rerun and give you timings.

> > - but one variance estimation (term sigma2.u3 below) is off by several orders of magnitude. I wonder if i erred in
> > porting my model code.

>

I was very surprised by that. think i erroneously inverted the individual parts of sigma as opposed to the matrix. that is hopefully the issue. thanks.

> > any optimization/reparameterization suggestions are welcome, but my first goal is getting results that make sense.
>
> Absolutely --- always debug first, optimize second.
>
> > Here is BUGS/JAGS code:
> >
> > |
> > model
> > {
> >   # Level 1 definition
> >   for(i in 1:N) {
> >        alpha[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i],tau)
> >
> >

> >   }
> >
> >
> >   # Higher level definitions

> >      u2[j] ~ dnorm(0,tau.u2)
> >   }

> >      u3[j,1:2] ~ dmnorm(zero3[1:2], tau.u3[1:2,1:2])
> >   }
> >
> >
> >   # Priors for fixed effects
> >   for (k in 1:18) { beta[k] ~ dflat() }
> >
> >
> >   # Priors for random terms
> >   tau ~ dgamma(0.001000,0.001000)
> >   sigma2 <- 1/tau
> >   tau.u2 ~ dgamma(0.001000,0.001000)
> >   sigma2.u2 <- 1/tau.u2
> >
> >
> >   for (i in 1:2) { zero3[i] <- 0 }
> >
> >
> >   tau.u3[1:2,1:2] ~ dwish(R3[1:2, 1:2],2)
> >   sigma2.u3[1:2,1:2] <- inverse(tau.u3[,])
> > }
> >
> >
> > |
> >
> > here is the STAN code:
> >
> > |
> > data {
> >      int<lower=1> N; //  number of rows
> >      int<lower=1> n2; // number of groups
> >      int<lower=1> n3; // number of individuals

> > }

> >
> >    cov_matrix[2] invR;
> >    invR <- inverse(R3);
>
> Inverse isn't very numerically stable, but should be OK here as long
> as R3 isn't too extreme.

R3 = matrix(c(0.002,0,0,0.002), nrow=2) so that should be fine.

>
> >    gamma_mu[1] <- 0;
> >    gamma_mu[2] <- 0;
>
> gamma_mu <- rep_vector(0.0,2);
>

ok.

> > }
> >
> > parameters {
> >   real<lower=-5, upper=5> beta[2];   // Priors for fixed effects (uniform)
>
> Is this a hard constraint?  If not, why not use a prior something like

I meant to provide a non-informative and produce the same output as MLwiN and BUGS, but i'll try that. it could help with numerical stability/speed?

> >   real u2[n2];
> >   vector[2] u3[n3];
> >
> >
> >   real<lower=0> sigmasq_u2; // Date-level vol

good catch, first one should be group-level

> >   cov_matrix[2] Sigma;
> >
> > }
> >
> >

> >    real<lower=0> sigma_u2;       // sigma in original bugs model
> >    real<lower=0> sigma_alpha;

messages.body_plain:
Yes, we drop constants from the lp__ calculations because they do not effect sampling.  Underneath the hood the contents can be recovered, but we do not include them in the lp__ output as that comes straight from the sampler.

On Aug 20, 2013, at 9:20 PM, Richard McElreath <rmcel...@gmail.com> wrote:

> I believe the built-in distributions are smart enough to drop constants from the lp__ calculations. There's some discussion of this on page 115 of the manual (1.3.0).
>
> That's my guess as to what is going on: the sqrt(pi) is not a function of a parameter (or transformed parameter yadda yadda), so it isn't added to lp__. If I'm right, if you do the updating manually with something like:
>
> lp__ <- lp__ + normal_log( x , mu , 1 );
>
> then the constant will be included and your back-of-envelop calculation will prove accurate.
>
> On Tuesday, August 20, 2013 12:56:44 PM UTC-7, John Tillinghast wrote:
> I'm trying to intepret lp__ for a super-simple model:
>
> normal_code <- '
>
> data {
>   int <lower=0> n;
>   real x[n];
> }
>
> parameters {
>   real mu;
> }
>
> model {
>   x ~ normal(mu, 1);
> }
>
> '
>
> But when I pass n=2, x=c(-1,1), I get lp__ = -1.489. This makes no sense to me.
>
> As I understand things, the Bayesian probability of mu should be proportional to exp( -1 - mu^2). Integrate wrt mu, and we get exp(-1) * sqrt(pi).
> Dividing, the posterior should be exp(-mu^2) / sqrt(pi), no? And at mu near 0, that would have lp ~ -0.57, no?
>
> What am I doing wrong here?

messages.body_plain:
We drop all the constant terms.  So when you write

   model {
     x ~ normal(mu, 1);
   }

with x a data vector and mu a parameter and sigma=1, you get this
for the log probability up to an additive constant:

    SUM_n  - 0.5 * (x[n] - mu)^2

which because sigma = 1, reduces to

    -0.5 * SUM_n (x[n] - mu)^2

The - log sigma^2 term is ignored, as is the sqrt(2 pi) and
sigma drops out of the denominator because it's a constant 1.

 > As I understand things, the Bayesian probability

The posterior p(mu|y) is proportional to p(y|mu) * p(mu).  And
because you have an improper uniform prior on mu, that works out
to be proportional to p(y|mu).

 > of mu should be proportional to exp( -1 - mu^2). Integrate wrt
 > mu, and we get exp(-1) * sqrt(pi).

I don't see why you want to integrate here.   To get the posterior
expectation, which is what should be reported by the mean of mu in
the output?

As to where the -1.49 comes from, it depends on what mu is,
and that will vary across samples.  Your example works out to:

     - 0.5 * ((1 - mu)^2 + (-1 - mu)^2)

because you have x = [-1 1].

- Bob

On 8/20/13 4:45 PM, John Tillinghast wrote:
> Right now I'm not even thinking of model comparison. I am comparing STAN with some other ways of calculating integrals.

Stan's only really set up to give you integrals in the
form of posterior expectations.

    E[f(theta)|y]

where f is an arbitrary function of the parameters theta
and the density of theta is the posterior p(theta|y).

> So the actual value of lp__ matters.
>
> The model and data are supposed to be ultra-trivial: two data points (-1 and 1). One parameter (mu, the mean of a normal
> distribution with sd=1).
>

>
> Is it really something else?

Our messages saying the same thing crossed.  But it is done
on the log scale.  So we calculate the expectation of

    - 0.5 * sum((x-mu)^2)

- Bob

On 8/20/13 4:07 PM, jb5 wrote:
>      > I've migrated a model from MLwiN to first BUGS and then JAGS and now STAN in hopes of overcoming memory
>     limitations and
>      > secondarily speeding estimation times.
>      > I get essentially similar estimated parameters from MLwiN, BUGS and JAGS. Stan runs fine - although not faster as
>     hoped
>      > for
>
>     How does the speed compare?  And are you running in R
>     or command-line and are you compiling Stan with full
>     optimization (O=3 on the command line or set_cppo("fast") in R).
>
>     We haven't fully optimized our multivariate models yet, so
>     the speed should continue to improve in future Stan releases
>     (I don't think there are improvements for speed for this
>     in Stan 2.0).
>
> I'm using rstan with set_cppo("fast"). I'll rerun and give you timings.

Thanks.

Also, are you using the same initial values?  By default, Stan starts
with very diffuse priors, whereas JAGS takes the mean and I believe
BUGS samples from the posterior.

Also, are you measuring effective samples per second, or just iteration
speed?   Only the former matters for inference and parameter estimation.
It's a bit tricky, because you need to use the same effective sample size
estimators to compare apples to apples, but R2WinBUGS and R2jags and RStan
use different estimators (I believe the former use something from Coda,
whereas RStan uses the within-across chain estimators described in our doc
and in the 3rd edition of Bayesian Data Analysis).

Next, there's time to converge, and then mixing speed after convergence.
HMC (as in Stan) tends to converge in fewer iterations from bad starting points than
Gibbs (as in BUGS/JAGS).

>      > - but one variance estimation (term sigma2.u3 below) is off by several orders of magnitude. I wonder if i erred in
>      > porting my model code.
>
>     The translation from sigma2.u3 to Sigma looks OK to me.
>
>     I wouldn't  expect one covariance parameter to be off without affecting
>     the others.
>
>     Could it be that you're comparing inverted with un-inverted matrices?
>
> I was very surprised by that. think i erroneously inverted the individual parts of sigma as opposed to the matrix. that
> is hopefully the issue. thanks.
>
>      > any optimization/reparameterization suggestions are welcome, but my first goal is getting results that make sense.
>
>     Absolutely --- always debug first, optimize second.
>
>      > Here is BUGS/JAGS code:
>      >
>      > |
>      > model
>      > {
>      >   # Level 1 definition
>      >   for(i in 1:N) {
>      >        alpha[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i],tau)
>      >
>      >

>      >   }
>      >
>      >
>      >   # Higher level definitions
>      >   for (j in 1:n2) {
>      >      u2[j] ~ dnorm(0,tau.u2)
>      >   }
>      >   for (j in 1:n3) {
>      >      u3[j,1:2] ~ dmnorm(zero3[1:2], tau.u3[1:2,1:2])
>      >   }
>      >
>      >
>      >   # Priors for fixed effects
>      >   for (k in 1:18) { beta[k] ~ dflat() }
>      >
>      >
>      >   # Priors for random terms
>      >   tau ~ dgamma(0.001000,0.001000)
>      >   sigma2 <- 1/tau
>      >   tau.u2 ~ dgamma(0.001000,0.001000)
>      >   sigma2.u2 <- 1/tau.u2
>      >
>      >
>      >   for (i in 1:2) { zero3[i] <- 0 }
>      >
>      >
>      >   tau.u3[1:2,1:2] ~ dwish(R3[1:2, 1:2],2)
>      >   sigma2.u3[1:2,1:2] <- inverse(tau.u3[,])
>      > }
>      >
>      >
>      > |
>      >
>      > here is the STAN code:
>      >
>      > |
>      > data {
>      >      int<lower=1> N; //  number of rows
>      >      int<lower=1> n2; // number of groups
>      >      int<lower=1> n3; // number of individuals
>      >      int<lower=0,upper=1> pred[N];
>      >      int<lower=1, upper=n2> group[N];
>      >      int<lower=1, upper=n3> id[N];
>      >      real alpha[N];
>      >
>      >      cov_matrix[2] R3;  // R3 = matrix(c(0.002,0,0,0.002), nrow=2)
>      >
>      >      int<lower=0,upper=1>    v_pred[N];
>      > }
>      >
>      > transformed data {

>      >
>      >    cov_matrix[2] invR;
>      >    invR <- inverse(R3);
>

>
>
> R3 = matrix(c(0.002,0,0,0.002), nrow=2) so that should be fine.

That should be fine and the overhead of the general inverse() call

>

>      >    gamma_mu[1] <- 0;
>      >    gamma_mu[2] <- 0;
>
>     gamma_mu <- rep_vector(0.0,2);
>
> ok.
>
>      > }

>

Right --- I'm assuming you'll convince yourself it's working with

> I'm familiar with andrew's paper. Given his preference for the half_cauchy, I was somewhat surprised to see the

in RStan or Stan.

I posted a response about this recently, but the
list is so high-volume I can't even find it.

It would be nice to have, but our recommendation is to
just restart.  Run 100 iterations, if that isn't enough,
run 200, and so on, until you get enough.  At most you'll
have to do about twice as much work as you would by
restarting, but you get the benefit of adaptation running
longer each time.

The practical reason we haven't implemented it is saving
all the adaptation and RNG state.  We have lots of adaptations
strategies, so there's not a standard way to do it, and the
Boost RNG we use do not support persistence.  (And we want
results to be reproducible, at least within a given version of (R)Stan.)

- Bob
