messages.body_plain:
We've been exploring the Matt trick more, and its efficacy
depends on the amount of data.  The less data there is, the
more effective it is.

The LKJ priors let you do things like shrink to the unit
correlation matrix and put independent priors on scale.  It's
a more natural prior than Wishart.  It's just as efficient in
Stan because we don't do anything special for conjugate priors.
Check out this paper by Ben Goodrich (who's done most of the
multivariate implementations in Stan).

We still haven't fully optimized our multivariate priors, so
they'll get substantially faster in the coming year (I'm guessing
an order of magnitude faster or more).

If the data's big, the time spent computing the likelihood will
dwarf the time spent computing the prior, so it doesn't really matter
what you use for efficiency.  Cholesky factoring in the model outside
of the likelihood loop can be a huge time saver.  That is, instead of

     for (n in 1:N)
       y[n] ~ multi_normal(mu,Sigma);

use something lik:

     {
        matrix[rows(Sigma),rows(Sigma)] L;
        L <- cholesky_decompose(Sigma);
        for (n in 1:N)
          y[n] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mu,L);
     }

The brackets provide the scope for the local variable L.

- Bob

>
>
> On 8/20/13 9:56 AM, Brendan wrote:
> > Cheers for the quick response Ben!
> >
> > Point taken with the count data. My main inferential interest is the probability that a new unit 'dies' in the next
> > year, so my thought process started with a logit. I'm also trying to build my intuition with Stan ahead of data coming
> > in, by trying lots of specifications with synthetic data. So, I'm afraid the answer to your question is 'No' :) .
> >
> > A Poisson type model with some allowance for overdispersion is a very good idea. I've tried to get at it in a couple of
> > ways, the least awful is below.
> >
> > I took the approach used in Gelman & Hill (p. 382) for overdispersion in BUGS, with Gaussian noise on the linear
> > predictor passed to the Poisson distribution function, and the lp__ incrementing method for censored data in the manual
> > (p. 45),
> >
> > |
> > model {
> >      mu ~ normal(0, 100);
> >      beta ~ normal(0, 100);
> >
> >      for(n in 1:N_obs)
> >          lambada_obs[n] ~ normal(mu + x_obs[n] * beta,  sigma);
> >
> >      y_obs ~ poisson_log(lambada_obs);
> >
> >      for(n in 1:N_cen)
> >          lambada_cen[n] ~ normal(mu + x_cen[n] * beta,  sigma);
> >
> >      lp__ <- lp__ + N_cen * log1m(poisson_cdf(L, lambada_cen));
> > }
> >
> > |
> >
> > ...where L (int <lower=0> L[N_cen]) is the lower bounds on the censored data. My intuition is that I should be
> > exponentiating the linear predictor before I pass it to the |poisson_cdf|, but Stan doesn't like the ways I've tried,
> > and either terminates the R session or throws out of bounds errors.
>
>
>
> >
> > Confusingly, it seems to estimate mu okay (with enough iterations), but seems to estimate beta and sigma very low. The
> > estimate of beta gets lower as the proportion of censored data gets higher, stepping over 2 SDs away from both the
> > parameter in the data generating mechanism, and the point estimate from a 'full obs only' model when censoring's ~50% of
> > data on a toy problem. When the proportion of censored data is relatively modest (~11%), beta looks okay, but sigma is
> > low,  > 2 SDs away from the 'obs only' estimate, and the parameter in the DGM.
> >
> > So, the specification above performs worse than an 'obs only' model on the same data set.
> >
> > Any ideas on where I've gone wrong?
> >
>
> Shouldn't that last line be:
>
>      for (n in 1:N_cen)
>        lp__ <- lp__ + log1m(poisson_cdf(L[n],lambda_cen[n]));
>
> That is, it's the ccdf function you want vectorized.
>
>
>      log Poisson_CCDF(L,lambda_cen)
>
>      = SUM_n log Poisson_CCDF(L[n],lambda_cen[n])
>
>      = SUM_n log1m(Poisson_CDF(L[n], lambda_cen[n]);
>
> What you have is:
>
>      log(1 - SUM_n log poisson_CDF(L[n], lambda_cen[n]);
>
> - Bob

current patches and pull requests for bug fixes and tweaks trickle through).

Thanks for the detailed report.  It's definitely a bug
on our side.  The behavior should be that anything that can
be translated by stanc should be compilable by g++ and clang++.

We're in the middle of changing how much of this works, but
your model's still problematic on our develop branch.  The problem
we get is in the optimizer instantiations.

I'll take a look and get back to you.

As to the speed, one issue you may be having is with the
odd prior for deviation parameters asig and bsig:

   parameters {
     ...
     real<lower=0> asig;
     real<lower=0> bsig;
     ...
   model {
     ...
     lp__ <- lp__ - log(asig) - log(bsig);
     ...

This is an improper prior taking on the linear scale (where
propto is multiplicative):

    p(asig) propto 1/asig

so that on the log scale (where propto is additive)

    log p(asig) propto -log(asig)

Is there a motivation for this prior?  And what happens to the
asig and bsig variables in terms of mixing and values?

- Bob

P.S.  The error novel output's tricky even for those of us with
       a couple of years of experience with C++ templates :-)  It's
       often useful to use both g++ and clang++ as their error reporting
       is quite different.

so that either the model you have will work, or you will get
a reasonable error message indicating that "add" is reserved.
I just filed an issue if you'd like to track our progress fixing:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/193

It will be fixed before 2.0 is out.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On Thursday, August 22, 2013 8:59:29 PM UTC-4, Nicholas Nagle wrote:
>
> I am running stan from R.  Here is a minimal script:
>
> stan_model <- '
> data{
>   int<lower=1> K; // number of variables
> }
> parameters{
>   matrix[K,K] L; // Cholesky factor of correlation matrix
> }

This L is going to be a dense K by K matrix. We do not yet have a type for the Cholesky factor of a correlation matrix, although there is a Cholesky factor of a covariance matrix in the next version of Stan.

> I was expecting the sampled matrices to 1) be lower triangular and 2) have Sigma=L*L' be a correlation matrix with ones on the diagonal.  The sampled matrices 'L' have neither of these properties.

In general, the densities that are used in the model {} block don't imply any restrictions on things in the parameters {} block, but in general the densities typically check whether the restrictions hold. The lkj_corr_cholesky() function doesn't actually check whether the input is lower triangular and that is basically because it was only intended to be used internally but accidentally got exposed to the Stan parser.  What is supposed to happen soon is to introduce a density on L such that L * L' is a correlation matrix with the LKJ density, which is probably what you were expecting.

> I also don't understand all the ":0"'s  in the printout, but that's probably a different topic.

Those are for the derivatives, which had not yet been evaluated when you printed L.

Ben

On 8/23/13 12:05 AM, Nicholas Nagle wrote:
>
>     In general, the densities that are used in the model {} block don't imply any restrictions on things in the
>     parameters {} block, but in general the densities typically check whether the restrictions hold. The
>     lkj_corr_cholesky() function doesn't actually check whether the input is lower triangular and that is basically
>     because it was only intended to be used internally but accidentally got exposed to the Stan parser.
>
>

> OK.  Thanks.  So, lkj_corr_cholesky should not be used at this time?

Right.

I don't think we can just Cholesky factor a correlation matrix,
because we won't be accounting for the Jacobian.  It really does
require us to have a correlation Cholesky factor type.

I just filed an issue to remove it from the function signatures for
2.0.

>     What is supposed to happen soon is to introduce a density on L such that L * L' is a correlation matrix with the LKJ
>     density, which is probably what you were expecting.
>
>

> Looking forward to this!  lkj_corr creates non-positive definite matrices too often for comfort and can take a
> relatively long time per iteration.  I was hoping to try out lkj_corr_cholesky, but it sounds like it's not ready.
>
> Again, thanks!

Just a note on what's going on under the hood.

We set things like step sizes to expect a certain amount of
rejection.  As long as it doesn't lead to too strong a correlation
in the output traceplots, it's OK in the sense that the posterior
samples are still drawn properly.

The non-positive definite matrices typically arise from arithmetic
issues in either underflow/overflow, non-transitivity of
addition [ (a + b) + c is not necessarily the same as a + (b + c)
in floating point ], and too large a step size in the Hamiltonian
dynamics simulation (which is intentional to get a good balance
between rejection and movement, just as in Metropolis sampling).

- Bob

> >     parameters {} block, but in general the densities typically check whether the restrictions hold. The

> >     because it was only intended to be used internally but accidentally got exposed to the Stan parser.

> > OK.  Thanks.  So, lkj_corr_cholesky should not be used at this time?
>
> Right.
>
> I don't think we can just Cholesky factor a correlation matrix,
> because we won't be accounting for the Jacobian.  It really does
> require us to have a correlation Cholesky factor type.
>
> I just filed an issue to remove it from the function signatures for
> 2.0.

The only situation in which it makes sense to use currently is:

parameters {
  corr_matrix[K] Sigma;
}
model {
  matrix[K,K] L;
  L <- cholesky_decompose(Sigma);
  L ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(eta); // implies: lkj_cor(eta) prior on Sigma
  // use L for some other calculation
}

This is a tiny bit faster (but more confusing) than just doing

Sigma ~ lkj_corr(eta);

because lkj_corr() internally calculates the Cholesky factor of Sigma in order to evaluate the determinant of Sigma. Worse, lkj_corr() also validates whether Sigma is, in fact, (numerically) positive definite, so it actually takes the Cholesky factorization twice.

But I don't know if avoiding that redundant calculation is worth the confusion, particularly if we soon add (to the confusion with) the density on L such that L * L' is a correlation matrix that is distributed LKJ with shape eta.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
On 8/23/13 3:15 PM, Chad Scherrer wrote:
> I have a hierarchical logistic regression model with a large number of observations, and a much smaller number of
> groups. Here's a very simplified version:
>
> |
> data {
>    vector[N] kk;
>    vector[N] x;
>    int<lower=0,upper=1> y[N];
> }
>
> parameters {
>    vector[K] a;
>    vector[K] b;
> }
>
> model {
>    vector[N] bn;
>
>    a ~ normal(0,100);
>    b ~ normal(0,100);
>
>    for(n in 1:N) {
>      an[n] <- a[kk[n]];
>      bn[n] <- b[kk[n]];
>    }
>

>    y ~ bernoulli_logit(an+ ... + x .* exp(bn + ...));

> }
> |
>
> It's vaguely similar to the model on page 56 of the Stan 1.3.0 manual. The "..." represent other terms similar to a and
> b that are also vectorized under the for loop. The exponential is to ensure that P(y|x) increases with x, though
> individual terms within the exponential may be very negative, corresponding to a flatter (but never decreasing) P(y|x)
> curve.

Does this make more sense than constraining the terms inside
exp() to be positive?

> Before vectorizing this, I had it running overnight and only had ~15 warmup samples by the morning. After I vectorized
> it, it ran in about 20 minutes. But then in trying to tune the model, I'm finding the execution time to be very
> unstable, and unpredictable.

What are you doing for initialization?

>   * In my "y ~ ..." line, is it ok that y is an array, but everything else is a vector? It's not clear to me whether the
>     two play nicely together.

Yes, that's fine.  When we write "reals" in the manual for an
argument in a signature, it can be a scalar or any one-dimensional
structure (array, vector, or row vector).  If there's more than one
array, vector or row vector, they all have to be the same size.
That's the only restriction.

>   * Any suggestions for getting faster and more predictable performance?

1.  Provide reasonable inits.

2.  Tighter priors (unless you reall do expect the a in a ~ normal(0,100)
to range between -300 and +300 or so).  You may also want to account for
covariance, as Andrew suggested.

RMHMC should be effective when there are large number of data
points and not so many (< 1000) parameters.  It deals with the
geometry issues of these hierarchical models.

>   * Have you found profiling (gprof, etc) helpful in situations like this, or is the result too far-removed from the

>     Stan code to be interpretable?

We know where the computation goes, so profiling per se isn't too
helpful (unless we find we've coded something badly, which profiling
can find).

Instead, Michael Betancourt's written a diagnostics package that
gets more at the geometry of the posterior.  What we want to see is if
there are places where lots of rejection happens (usually high curvature)
or spots in the posterior where the sampler's getting stuck, correlations
among the parameters.  The biggest problem is posterior scale variation
coupled with correlation.

Some reparameterizations can help here, like the "Matt trick".
Especially in cases of little data.

> My last question is very different. Since N is large (about half a million), it makes some sense to speed things up by
> taking a subset of the data. I hate to just throw away data in a final result, so I'd have to find a way to run a few
> models and somehow connect them after the fact. The whole thing seems a bit flaky.

We've thought about that even in just a simple linear regression case,
but there's the issue of how to scale the priors and then how to combine them.
We'd love to hear other thoughts on this.

Over the next year, we're hoping to get stochastic variational inference
working, which will only deal with part of the data at a time (providing
essentially a subgradient with expecation equal to full gradient).  We're
working directly with the authors of this paper:

   Stochastic Variational Inference
   Matthew D. Hoffman, David M. Blei, Chong Wang, John Paisley;
   JMLR 2013.
   http://jmlr.org/papers/v14/hoffman13a.html

Matt's the one who developed the NUTS sampler and also explored
reparameterizations.

> This makes me wonder about the possibility of each iteration choosing a random (or hashed, or something) subset of the N
> observations. This could make things go much faster, and it seems there could be connections to online algorithms. But
> I'm not sure if there would need to be a correction factor at runtime or after the fact to account for not using all of
> the data. And random number generation is only available in "generated quantities", so I'd need a hack of some sort. Any
> thoughts on this?

Yes!  See the above.  I don't know if we'll figure it out for MCMC,
but we do hope to get it working for variational inference.

- Bob

PS:  Did you try Passage (or another Gibbs sampler) on this model?

On Saturday, August 24, 2013 3:04:34 PM UTC-4, Nicholas Nagle wrote:
> OK.  I got that.  That worked like a charm.  I'm not sure if it is appreciably faster than lkj_corr, but it doesn't throw thousands of positive definite errors.  I know it's unreasonable to place more faith in a model that is quiet, but that's about the size of it.

The reason lkj_corr_choleksy() doesn't throw warnings and should be somewhat faster than lkj_corr() is that lkj_corr() checks whether its argument is in fact a correlation matrix (symmetric, unit diagonal, positive definite) whereas lkj_corr_cholesky() doesn't check anything, not even that its argument is lower-triangular. This is dangerous because if lkj_corr_cholesky() were called on anything other than a Cholesky factor of a correlation matrix, it would yield the wrong answer. It would also yield the wrong answer if you manually constructed an L such that L * L' is a correlation matrix unless you also manually made the Jacobian correction for the change-of-variables from the correlations to the free elements of L. But we do want to automate that once we make it possible to declare a parameter as a Cholesky factor of a correlation matrix.

> lkj_corr_cholesky seems like magic to me.  I don't see how lkj_corr_cholesky can know that L - which is defined as a regular matrix[K,K] - is also related to a corr_matrix, but it does.

There's no magic. It doesn't know anything really. It just depends on the caller only calling lkj_corr_cholesky() when that conditional holds, which is why it was a mistake to expose that function (which was intended to only be used internally) to the Stan language that users write models in.

Ben

I was on vacation, but I'm back on my packaging r/stan for Debian
project.

Once rstan is installed on a system what does it need to operate?
In particular, does it need the boost, eigen, or stan headers?
Clearly it needs the C compiler and the stan library, though I'm a
little confused about whether it uses the static or dynamic one; both
are in the makefile.

There are actually 3 different phases:
stanc (exported as a function for rstan) creates cc source file.
the cc file produced by stanc is compiled
the compiled file is run.

I've speculated that the static and dynamic libraries might be used in
different phases, but I haven't traced it through.

This matters because Debian has two types of dependency relations,
build-depends and depends.  build-depends are requirements to build the
package, which corresponds to everything through R CMD INSTALL.  Then
someone on a different machine can install the binary (Debian) package
and use it.  It's good to keep the depends and build-depends lists as
minimal as possible.

Ross Boylan

messages.body_plain:
Because bin/stanc generates code which gets compiled, the
terminology "run time" and "compile time" are relative.

Stan compiles the following three targets.  The first two
are executables, so you don't need anything else once they're made:

1.   bin/stanc
2.   bin/print

The third is an archive, which is used later for compiling models:

3.  bin/libstan.a

Then, at "run time", bin/stanc is executed and passed
a new Stan model files to generate a .cpp file for the model.

This leads to a fourth compile target.

4.a. For the command line, the model's .cpp file is compiled with a main()
and generates an executable that can then be run run.

4.b. In R, the model.cpp is compiled dynamically without a main()
method [bin/stanc is configured not to generate a main]
and then the the dynamic object file is linked in using whatever
magic Rcpp, inline and R give us.

All four compiles involve the headers for Boost and Eigen.  We
probably could get away without Eigen in building bin/stanc.

- Bob

- radon.nopooling.stan (2nd model in "16.5_Bugs_codes.bug")

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Slow hierarchical logistic regression
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Slow hierarchical logistic regression
messages.body_plain:
On Fri, Aug 23, 2013 at 6:59 PM, Chad Scherrer <chad.s...@gmail.com> wrote:

> On Friday, August 23, 2013 12:25:56 PM UTC-7, Marcus wrote:
> > The speed variations are most likely due to differences in starting point.  Chains which fail to mix or mix slowly likely started in a really bad part of the space and are having trouble escaping or adapted poorly.  One possible work around for the adaptation problem is to allow for a longer warmup.  Fixing initializations is a little hard right now (we have a bunch of things planned to fix it in the future though!).  One option is to manually specify your initializations.  If you want to run multiple chains for Rhat statistics, then you can create multiple initializations for each chain manually.
>
> Ahh, this makes sense. So maybe start with a point estimate, and feed that in for the initialization value. Since Stan already computes all the gradients, it would be great to see a future version allowing something like conjugate gradient, and reporting that value before using it for initialization.

In develop there is an implementation of the BFGS optimizer which should work pretty well.  That said, as others have pointed out I wouldn't recommend the point estimate in general however, logistic regression problems are generally convex so it should work well in this case.

Here are a couple of other options just in case:

- Use init=0 to initialize everything to a single point.
- If you only want to run one chain, take note of the random seed on one of the chains that seemed to work well and use that.
- Alternatively, generate several diffuse initializations.  Throw out the ones that have issues and manually specify from those curated random initializations.

>
> > Regarding using only subsets of data, this can theoretically be done in HMC in a very nice way by using a different simulation Hamiltonian but currently Stan doesn't support this.  I'm not sure if it's really in the pipe either, but it's a good idea for handing models with really large amounts of data.
>
> Cool! Except when I'm writing a paper, "That's already been done" is always the best response. Do you have any citations for similar work?

Check out section 5.5 of http://arxiv.org/pdf/1206.1901.pdf which talks about using an approximate Hamiltonian.  That approximate Hamiltonian could be constructed by using a subset of the data.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.body_plain:
I'd like to request a feature. Hierarchical models tend to have a sparse Hessian, and the trustOptim <http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/trustOptim/vignettes/trustOptim-vignette.pdf> R package gives fast optimization, based on a specification of the sparsity structure of the Hessian. This can be determined from the dependency graph of the model. Having this graph structure available for a given Stan model could, for example, lead to much faster Laplace approximations.

I'm not familiar with Stan's C++ code. But the graph we want is essentially that there is an edge between two variables if those variables occur together in a term of the log posterior. Is this readily available, or do you have any feel for how difficult this would be to extract and export to R? Any plans for this or anything similar already in the works?

Thanks,
Chad

On 8/28/13 11:35 AM, Chad Scherrer wrote:
> I'd like to request a feature. Hierarchical models tend to have a sparse Hessian, and the trustOptim

> <http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/trustOptim/vignettes/trustOptim-vignette.pdf> R package gives fast optimization,

> based on a specification of the sparsity structure of the Hessian. This can be determined from the dependency graph of
> the model. Having this graph structure available for a given Stan model could, for example, lead to much faster Laplace
> approximations.
>
> I'm not familiar with Stan's C++ code. But the graph we want is essentially that there is an edge between two variables
> if those variables occur together in a term of the log posterior. Is this readily available, or do you have any feel for
> how difficult this would be to extract and export to R? Any plans for this or anything similar already in the works?

The problem is that there's no notion of graphical model behind
Stan.  It's just a log probability function that's proportional
to the posterior p(theta|y) where theta are params and y is data.
This can be structured like a directed graphical
model for the joint p(y,theta), but there's nothing in the language
that lets us extract the (implicit) graph.

We also don't have any sparse matrix algebra plugged in, though
Eigen's added a bunch more support and brought it into the mainstream
of their package.  I know almost nothing about the math behind this,
so I'm not the right person to ask about our doing this any time soon.
It's definitely relevant to other things we're doing, too, like
Riemann Manifold HMC, which might have a structured sparse Hessian which could
greatly speed up some of the algebraic operations.

- Bolb

I have a somewhat related question. First, let's assume I know nothing about HMC/NUTS, and am using Stan simply because it is a shiny new tool (which isn't that far from the truth...).

I have a model whose MCMC has a dimension changing reversible jump step (with which I assume Stan would have difficulty). Currently, I run the RJ step every K iterations of MCMC (usually about 10-100), and use MH sampling (implemented in Rcpp) for everything else. It's very slow to converge, something I was hoping Stan might remedy. Thus I was thinking of doing this:

1. Run Stan for K iterations
2. Outside of Stan, do the RJ step
3. Run Stan for another K iterations, initializing the parameters at the values where the previous Stan run ended
4. Repeat 2 and 3 until convergence

Now, for my questions. Is this a good idea for HMC in general? Stan in particular?
Given Bob's previous response, and assuming this is reasonable in HMC, how should I approach this? Run with standard HMC instead of NUTS? (NUTS is where the adaptation occurs, correct?)

Sorry if my description isn't clear. Any help would be appreciated!

Stan (and NUTS in particular) can be used without adaptation which is probably how you'd want to use it here.  You can specify the stepsize parameter by hand (or adapt it somehow outside of Stan and fix it for each run) and then turn off warmup/adaptation when you run Stan to try to do what you're proposing.  It's likely to work much better than MH assuming you can find reasonable settings for the stepsize parameter.

Cheers,
Marcus

Don't we run into undecidability issues?  We also have intermediate
values that can be calculated to determine loop indices and we
also have iterations (like for and while loops) that lead to
problems.

One thing I've thought about is supporting a more restrictive modeling
language for which we can compute these things.  These are all issues
for doing discrete sampling, where we want to somehow compute the Markov
blanket of a discrete variable.

messages.subject: Sampling from multivariate normal
messages.subject_clean: Sampling from multivariate normal
messages.body_plain:
Dear STANsters,

First, thanks for developing an exciting and well-designed and well-documented tool for Bayesian sampling.

I would like to use STAN to estimate parameters that are nestled inside of the mean and variance-covariance matrix of a multi-variate normal distribution, i.e. X ~ MVN(Mu(theta), Sigma(theta)), where "thetas" are the parameters and the likelihood is just the probability density of the data vector X.  I am using STAN from within R, and the ultimate objective is to develop a package that obtains these estimates (and C.I.'s) from data.

As a simplistic example, I attach an example [.stan and .r files] where I estimate the autocorrelation coefficient rho of an AR(1) process by using the variance-covariance of the complete time-series [i.e. Sigma[i,j] = rho^(abs(i-j))].  This is not the best way to estimate rho, but it is exactly the template I'm looking for.

I got this to work, but have several questions.  (I am a bit of a novice here, so apologize in advance if the answers are well-known or documented elsewhere - I really did dig around):

1) The compilation worked using "set_cppo("fast")", but it would not compile using "set_cppo("debug")", giving me a non-specific error, with only a Cygwin POSIX path warning.  How/why is that possible?  It takes quite a while to compile - and if the "debug" is faster [plus more informative output], then that would be much more convenient for development.

2) I see that the compiled C++ code is stored somewhere deep (Users/eli/AppData/Temp/Local ... etc.) with some complicated auto-generated name. I couldn't figure out how to control where that code goes or how it is named.  A further question: Will it eventually be straightforward to implement the compiled C++ code in an R package via Rcpp (which is the ultimate goal)?

3) If there are any comments on the optimality/efficiency of the "stan" code for sampling from the MVN itself, they would be appreciated.  For the desired application, speed is highly desired.

Thanks,
- Eli

> likelihood is just the probability density of the data vector X.  I am using STAN from within R, and the ultimate
> objective is to develop a package that obtains these estimates (and C.I.'s) from data.

So it's like a Gaussian process example where Mu and Sigma are
functions of parameters?  There are some examples in the manual.

> As a simplistic example, I attach an example [.stan and .r files] where I estimate the autocorrelation coefficient rho
> of an AR(1) process by using the variance-covariance of the complete time-series [i.e. Sigma[i,j] = rho^(abs(i-j))].
>   This is not the best way to estimate rho, but it is exactly the template I'm looking for.
>
> I got this to work, but have several questions.  (I am a bit of a novice here, so apologize in advance if the answers
> are well-known or documented elsewhere - I really did dig around):
>
> 1) The compilation worked using "set_cppo("fast")", but it would not compile using "set_cppo("debug")", giving me a
> non-specific error, with only a Cygwin POSIX path warning.  How/why is that possible?

set_cppo("fast") sets C++ compiler
optimization to level 3 and set_cppo("debug") makes
it optimization level 0.  The current Stan (1.3.0) also uses set_cppo("fast")
to turn off some error handling, leading to potential R crashes.

In 2.0, the options will only set optimization and not error handling.

The problem is the C++ toolchain on Windows, which typically runs out
of memory or just dies when setting optimization level 0.

 > It takes quite a while to compile
 > - and if the "debug" is faster [plus more informative output], then
 > that would be much more convenient for development.

We don't want to rely on error messages from C++, but rather catch
them in Stan directly.  The debug version won't have more informative
output as far as Stan's concerned.

> 2) I see that the compiled C++ code is stored somewhere deep (Users/eli/AppData/Temp/Local ... etc.) with some
> complicated auto-generated name. I couldn't figure out how to control where that code goes or how it is named.

Why would you want to control this?

Jiqiang should be able to help if you really need to control it.

> A
> further question: Will it eventually be straightforward to implement the compiled C++ code in an R package via Rcpp
> (which is the ultimate goal)?

I'm not sure what you mean by "implement the compiled C++ code".

You can use the command-line version of Stan to compile the C++
code for a model and then do whatever you want with it.  But the I/O
is tricky given the constraints.

> 3) If there are any comments on the optimality/efficiency of the "stan" code for sampling from the MVN itself, they
> would be appreciated.  For the desired application, speed is highly desired.

We're working on making multivariate normal faster in a few different
ways.  One, we'll vectorize the distributions, and two, we'll support
Cholesky factor representations everywhere.  For now, Ben and Marcus have
provided a lot of examples on the mailing list.  But the basic idea is
to do the heavy lifting outside of a loop as much as possible.  So rather than

  for (n in 1:N)   y[n] ~ multi_normal(mu,Sigma);

which causes Sigma to be solved in every iteration, you can do something like:

  L <- cholesky_decompose(Sigma);
  for (n in 1:N) y[n] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mu,L);

- Bob

For an AR(1) model, I think you should pretty much never use the covariance matrix. Define a "cov_matrix" that is actually the inverse of the covariance matrix, which will be tridiagonal and is know analytically as a function of rho and sigma. Then call multi_normal_prec(). Ben

Thanks for your comment Ben,

> For an AR(1) model, I think you should pretty much never use the covariance matrix. Define a "cov_matrix" that is actually the inverse of the covariance matrix, which will be tridiagonal and is know analytically as a function of rho and sigma. Then call multi_normal_prec(). Or define the Cholesky factor of the precision matrix, which is bidiagonal, and manually increment the log-posterior in the model{} block.

I'm aware that this is a ridiculous way to estimate rho for an AR(1) - but it is a perfect minimal template for my actual problem.  In the real thing, the inverse matrix is unfortunately not a trivial function of the parameters ... but it should (I think) be somewhat sparse, in which case numerically using "multi_normal_prec()" may be faster.  I'll try that when I weave it all together.

Let me reiterate that implementing this estimation in STAN has been a smooth and (relatively) pleasant process!   It estimates well, is faster than anything a hack like myself could ever code, and the syntax / workflow / implementation is smooth and very transparent (e.g. only took me a couple of hours from downloading rstan to getting the AR(1) example working).   So kudos again on a great tool.  Am looking forward to watching it evolve.

Best,
- Eli

messages.body_plain:
I have an IRT model with priors that are a bit too vague
to identify it well in the posterior.  I fit using
RStan 1.3 and all the traceplots look like the one attached.
This one is 2000 iterations, but after adaptation ends,
the chain gets relatively frozen.

This one's for the intercept (equivalently hierarchical
mean), and it should have a value of around 1.0.

(As an aside, I reran the model for 5K iterations and everything
was fine, though the posterior intervals were very fat.)

Did perhaps a round of adaptation kick in at 1000 iterations to
reduce the step size dramatically?

Daniel was seeing identical kinds of behavior on a very different
model.  Everything appeared to be mixing during warmup, then
adaptation ends, and bang, a frozen chain.  (Daniel ran 4 chains
and 3 of them were OK.)

This is an issue that looks like a computational issue.  It's not
like it's frozen way out in some mode somewhere.

I haven't tested in 2.0, but I'm hoping the new adaptation will be a
bit better behaved.

- Bob

The problem is that block.hpp doesn't include validate_column_index.hpp.
It's been fixed already on the develop branch.

The puzzle isn't so much why it doesn't work on some platforms, but
how it worked on any platforms.

Here's the buggy 1.3 file, which is missing an include.

src/stan/math/matrix/block.hpp
============================================================
#ifndef __STAN__MATH__MATRIX__BLOCK_HPP__
#define __STAN__MATH__MATRIX__BLOCK_HPP__

#include <stan/math/matrix/Eigen.hpp>
#include <stan/math/matrix/validate_row_index.hpp>

namespace stan {
   namespace math {

     /**
      * Return a nrows x ncols submatrix starting at (i,j).
      *
      * @param m Matrix
      * @param i Starting row
      * @param j Starting column
      * @param nrows Number of rows in block
      * @param ncols Number of columns in block
      **/
     template <typename T>
     inline
     Eigen::Matrix<T,Eigen::Dynamic,Eigen::Dynamic>
     block(const Eigen::Matrix<T,Eigen::Dynamic,Eigen::Dynamic>& m,
           size_t i, size_t j, size_t nrows, size_t ncols) {
       validate_row_index(m,i,"block");
       validate_row_index(m,i+nrows-1,"block");
       validate_column_index(m,j,"block");
       validate_column_index(m,j+ncols-1,"block");
       return m.block(i - 1,j - 1,nrows,ncols);
     }

   }
}
#endif

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I ran into a problem cloning stan as a submodule of rstan:

--8<---------------cut here---------------start------------->8---
tamas@tamas:~/src$ git submodule update --init
Submodule 'stan' () registered for path 'stan'
remote: Counting objects: 83922, done.
remote: Compressing objects: 100% (36273/36273), done.
error: RPC failed; result=18, HTTP code = 200MiB | 233 KiB/s
fatal: The remote end hung up unexpectedly
fatal: early EOF
fatal: index-pack failed
Unable to fetch in submodule path 'stan'
--8<---------------cut here---------------end--------------->8---

I looked for solutions, but two of them need a repack/gc on the repo, so
I tried the third one [1]:

--8<---------------cut here---------------start------------->8---
tamas@tamas:~/src/rstan$ git config --global http.postBuffer 5242880000
--8<---------------cut here---------------end--------------->8---

which should be plenty, but I still get the same error.

My knowledge of git is superficial; any help would be appreciated.

Best,

Tamas

[1] http://stackoverflow.com/questions/17683295/git-bash-error-rpc-failed-result-18-htp-code-200b-1kib-s

People kept saying to me that a sampler needs to explore the full space fairly thoroughly, so I tried to do a plot which would help to show this by plotting four sub-samples of 50 consecutive points (duplicates removed) from a given chain.  In the case of my simple  stan model, with only two parameters, it appears that 50 plot points is not really enough to explore the full region - but 50 is getting towards the limit of a visible path when plotted.  Refer attached pdf plot.

Refer to https://github.com/seanpor/RStanGraphics

For the purpose of demonstration I have put a fit object on github, and to use the function you just need to do something like...

source('stanGgplot.R')
# if you don't already have a fit object handy you could use this one
fit <- readRDS('sample_banana_fit_object.rds')
stanPathPlot(fit)

It is still early days on this, but I thought I'd share now.  Constructive feedback is most welcome.

Kind regards,

Sean O'Riordain
Trinity College,
Dublin

On 8/30/13 4:51 AM, Sean O'Riordain wrote:
> Good morning from Dublin,

> I would be interested in your feedback on some ggplot2 work I've been doing with an rstan fit object.  People kept
> saying to me that a sampler needs to explore the full space fairly thoroughly,

Technically, it just needs to explore the space in proportion
to its posterior probability mass.  For example, normal(0,1)
has support on (-inf,inf), but you're never going to see samples
outside of (-4,4) unless you do a whole lot of sampling.

How many samples you need practically depends on what you're
trying to estimate.  If you're trying to estimate Pr(Y > 4)
accurately for some Y ~ normal(0,1), you're going to need a whole
lot more samples than if you're trying to estimate mean(Y) or
sd(Y).

> so I tried to do a plot which would help
> to show this by plotting four sub-samples of 50 consecutive points (duplicates removed) from a given chain.  In the case
> of my simple  stan model, with only two parameters, it appears that 50 plot points is not really enough to explore the
> full region - but 50 is getting towards the limit of a visible path when plotted.  Refer attached pdf plot.

That looks pretty good for the banana distribution.

You should take a look at Michael Betancourt's work on diagnostics in:

https://github.com/stan-dev/visual-diagnostics

If you could port some of Michael's diagnostics from gnuplot to ggplot2, it would
do all of us who use RStan a huge favor.  The next release of Stan (2.0), should
also have a bit more built-in support for reporting diagnostic info like the
derivatives, which are very important for seeing what's going on with HMC (I'm not
positive about this, but Michael will know, since he wrote that, too).  There's more
info in his arXiv papers with examples.

Right.  We followed the convention in the Eigen software
library.  We hope to add the MATLAB-style low:high notation
in a future release.  It actually shouldn't be too hard the
way things are abstracted now.

> Also, if I have a matrix C which just one row (1x10, for example), and I want the elements 6:10 (1x5), I would write
> block(C,1,6,1,5). Is this correct?

Yes, that's right if you have a 1 x 10 matrix.

In Stan, you should use a row-vector type for a (1 x 10) matrix.
But unfortunately, Stan 1.3 doesn't yet support the slicing
operations for vectors.  In Stan 2.0, if rv is a row vector,
you can do tail(rv,5) to return the last five elements as a row
vector.

Now having said that, a loop in Stan isn't going to be any slower
than a block operation, but it won't have the error checking of
the block() or tail() operations.

If you have another reason (other than slicing) for wanting
a 1 x 10 matrix, we'd like to know why, because it may reflect
a shortcoming in the way we do type inference or the set of matrix
operations we support.

- Bob

messages.subject: packaging plans
messages.subject_clean: packaging plans
messages.body_plain:
Here's my current thinking about how to package r/stan.  Comments welcome.

The first part of the changes involve stuff that is not Debian-specific,
though it may be Unix-specific.  I'll make a configure.ac <http://configure.ac> that looks for
the libraries currently used in several places, starting with where they
are now in the tarball.  This way they should work fine as things stand
now, but they will allow using libraries and headers that are already on
the system.

It doesn't look as if the current stan system uses configure, and that
many configure like operations (e.g., discovering the type of compiler)
are done in the makefiles.  So I wonder a bit if introducing configure
is a good idea, though it seems to me the natural way to approach the
problem of discovering libraries.  I'm also not sure how portable this
is to windows.

Then, getting into the Debian specific stuff, I'll strip out the
external headers from the stan and make at least one package that
contains the headers (stan-dev) and depends on other packages that
provide boost and eigen (also g++).  stan-dev might contain everything
else (e.g., compiled stanc), or there might be a stan package too.  My
interest is in rstan, and it's the stan headers I need for rstan.

The rstan package would similarly start from source with the external
headers, including the stan headers, removed.  It too would have a
configure script for finding those headers, and it would depend on those
headers, including stan-dev.

r/stan is a bit unusual.  For the generic package foo, the foo package
holds the executable, used by the user at run-time, and foo-dev holds
headers and libraries that a developer who was using the package would
need at compile time.  But for stan, run time is compile time, although
different things are compiled for the user (namely their .stan programs)
than for the "adminstrator" (e.g., stanc or the equivalent R library).

I looked a little to see if there is, or could be, a common stan library
used by stan and rstan.  That is, could there be a librstan that uses
libstan?  rstan/rstan/rstan/src seems to be the only rstan specific C++
code, and the files there are mostly versions of ones found in the stan
tree (after translating names like a_b_c to a/b/c).  Some of them are
clearly different: stanc.cpp and chains.cpp have R interfaces.  Others
have only an include line that refers to the equivalent stan file.  This
suggests that at least in principle rstan could depend on stan
libraries.  The simplest path for now is likely for the rstan package to
rely on stan-dev only for headers.

Ross

The preferred way in debian-land is *not* to put debian stuff in the
"upstream" stan source at all (not even inside a debian/ folder). It
all gets applied downstream. Debian maintainers can then look after
the debian-specific customisations without having to (for example)
have access to the stan repo. If I read right, Ross is going with that
approach - i.e. the main stan repo won't see any changes.

Dan

If y are the unconstrained values and x = f(y) are
the constrained values, then if you write

    x ~ foo(theta);

you need to add the log of the absolute determinant of
the Jacobian matrix for the transform f.  The entries
J[m,n] in the Jacobian are:

   J[m,n] = d/d.y[m]  { f(y)[n] }

I don't understand the intent of what you're doing, but you
have two priors on the matrix, one from the sampling statement on
logit_r1 and one from the sampling statement on phi.

If you just put the priors on phi, you can transform and use
the result as a parameter w/o a Jacobian adjustment.  If you drop
the priors on phi and go with a prior on logit_r1, then you'll need
the Jacobian of the transform.  If you leave them both, it's essentially
a product prior.

    a ~ foo(theta);
    a ~ bar(rho);

means

   p(a) propto foo(a|theta) * bar(a|rho);

It doesn't look like the derivatives are too bad, but
all the indexing looks like it's going to be fiddly unless
you can reexpress in terms of simpler vectors.

- Bob

On 8/31/13 2:44 AM, Sean O'Riordain wrote:

> "unlikely" :-)

I didn't see that in the plot --- it looked like you were getting both.

The banana's pretty tricky because there's no global
adaptation that Stan can do in terms of either a diagonal
or full mass matrix that makes sense because the correlation
structure is different in different parts of the banana.  The best
you can do with Stan's current implementation is to find a small
enough scale that you can do a kind of random walk.

RMHMC does a much better job.

We should probably list this as one of our test examples since everybody
seems to like it.

> What I've been doing is running this plot a few times to see if the chains are getting "stuck".
>
> I will start on the translation of Michaels gnuplot code to ggplot2 on Monday morning first thing - shall I just put
> them in my github repository so you can take them from there?

That'll certainly work for now.

I think we'd eventually like to roll something like this into RStan
directly if you'd be willing to BSD license what you're doing.

The reason it's now standalone is that Michael's using gnuplot rather
than R, so it doesn't fit into RStan, and the GNU license is not
a dependency we want in the core Stan distribution.

- Bob
